samples.hyp:
of the potential impact of temperature on the COVID-19 epidemic in Australia
In this study, we construct a simple mathematical model to describe the COVID-19 outbreak in Australia and use it to explore the potential impact of temperature on the epidemic. The model is a modified version of a SEIR (susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered) model that incorporates a seasonality forcing term with the temperature as a potential driver of COVID-19 viral load. Further, we incorporate age-structure into the model to account for the increased susceptibility of the elderly to the infection. Our results indicate that temperature can have a significant impact on the COVID-19 epidemic. A higher mean daily temperature was associated with a lower daily new case count and a shorter doubling time of the epidemic. However, the effect of temperature on the epidemic is moderated by the age-structure of the population. For younger populations with a lower proportion of the elderly, temperature has a stronger effect on reducing the epidemic size, while for older populations with a larger proportion of the elderly, temperature has a weaker effect on reducing the epidemic size. Our results also suggest that the effect of temperature on reducing the epidemic size is more pronounced in areas with a lower mean daily new case count. These findings add to growing evidence that temperature can have a significant impact on the spread of COVID-19 and highlight the importance of considering the local age-structure of the population in public health interventions.
COVID-19, Mathematical modelling, Temperature, Age-structure
The COVID-19 pandemic has affected countries all around the world, with the total number of cases worldwide constantly on the rise [1]. The outbreak has also had significant impacts on Australian society, with over 27,000 confirmed cases and over 900 deaths as of 1 October 2020 [2]. As the number of confirmed cases has grown, the Australian government has implemented a range of public health interventions, including social distancing, border closures, and a mandatory quarantine period for international travellers [3]. The effectiveness of these interventions has led to the de-escalation of the lockdown and the re-opening of businesses and schools across Australia. However, with restrictions being eased and the number of cases beginning to rise again in some states, it is important to understand the potential drivers of COVID-19 transmission in Australia. However, the role of asymptomatic infection in the spread of COVID-19 in Africa is poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of asymptomatic infection in the spread of COVID-19 in Africa using a data-driven mathematical model. We show that the role of asymptomatic infection in the spread of COVID-19 in Africa is substantial. We predict that in the absence of control measures, the number of infections in Africa between April and October 2020 could be 4.3 to 6.6 times higher than the number of confirmed infections. We also show that a substantial number of infections in Africa are mild, leading to a lower case fatality rate than what has been observed in other parts of the world. Our results suggest that the role of asymptomatic infection in the spread of COVID-19 in Africa should be fully considered in African countries as they develop and implement control strategies for COVID-19.

samples.src: We developed a simplified deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to assess the effect of active isolation of SARS-CoV-2 infected but asymptomatic individuals through blanket testing for control of the outbreak in Lusaka Province of Zambia.
samples.ref: Senze imodeli yezibalo eyenziwe lula ye-deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) ukuhlola umthelela wokuhlukaniswa okusebenzayo kwabantu abatheleleke nge-SARS-CoV-2 kodwa abangenazimpawu ngokuhlola ingubo yokulawula ukuqubuka kwesiFundazwe saseLusaka eZambia.
samples.hyp:
The model incorporates the novel coronavirus transmission dynamics with a latent period, and the effects of control strategies including contact tracing, isolation and quarantine. The model's parameters were estimated using data from the COVID-19 outbreak in Lusaka and elsewhere. The model was fitted to the daily new cases in Lusaka showing a good fit. The estimated R0 of the COVID-19 outbreak in Lusaka was 2.97 indicating that the first wave of the outbreak in Lusaka was not contained. However, the estimated effective reproductive number, R, of 1.54 when active isolation of infected and pre-symptomatic individuals was included in the model suggests that the ongoing mass testing and isolation of cases is bringing the epidemic under control. We estimate that without the ongoing mass testing, the number of daily new cases would be 210, which is much higher than the 16 daily new cases observed in Lusaka. Our analysis shows that the number of daily new cases in Lusaka would start decreasing 21 days after the onset of active isolation of infected and pre-symptomatic individuals, and that the number of daily new cases would eventually reach zero and remain at zero if active isolation is sustained. However, if active isolation is stopped after achieving a 95% reduction in the number of daily new cases, the number of daily new cases would rise again and would exceed pre-isolation levels if the reproduction number is not kept below 1.0. If the reproduction number rises to 2.5 the number of daily new cases would exceed 2000 per day. The model results show that it is important to maintain a high level of active surveillance and case isolation to prevent a resurgence of the outbreak. It is also important to develop and apply effective strategies for tracing and isolating contacts of infected and pre-symptomatic individuals to reduce the spread of the disease.

The first scenario, of equally infectious asymptomatic individuals, represents the worst-case scenario and was estimated to be associated with a 65% IFR, compared with a 53% IFR when the model assumed that asymptomatic individuals were only half as infectious as symptomatic individuals. This difference suggests that the assumption of asymptomatic individuals being less infectious than symptomatic individuals has a substantial effect on the estimated IFR. However, both scenarios represent IFRs that are substantially higher than the 0.2% to 0.4% IFR estimated for SARS-CoV-2 in the general population in China. This difference could be due to several factors, including the possibility that the contact patterns in South Africa are different from those in China, resulting in different IFRs. Alternatively, it could be the case that the South African health system is better able to diagnose and treat COVID-19 than the health system in China, where the case fatality rate was approximately 3.5%.13

samples.src: Our model predicts that active isolation of COVID-19 cases, including asymptomatic individuals, through blanket testing can be used as a possible measure for the control of the SARS-Cov-2 transmission in Lusaka, Zambia, but it would come at a high cost.
samples.ref: Imodeli yethu ibikezela ukuthi ukuhlukaniswa okusebenzayo kwamacala e-COVID-19, okubandakanya abantu abangenazimpawu, ngokuhlolwa kwengubo kungasetshenziswa njengesinyathelo sokulawula ukudluliswa kwe-SARS-Cov-2 eLusaka, eZambia, kodwa kuzofika ngezindleko eziphezulu.
samples.hyp:
The model was used to estimate the prevalence of the disease in Lusaka and predict the impact of testing on the prevalence of the disease. We assumed that the reproduction number (R) was reduced to 1 during the testing period. The prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in Lusaka was estimated to be 6.89% with 95% confidence interval (5.63%, 8.48%). Our model projects that a one-week testing of 1,732,684 individuals in Lusaka will lead to a reduction of the prevalence to 0.94% (95% confidence interval: 0.71%, 1.24%) after allowing for a 2-week period for the remaining infected individuals to leave the isolation facilities. This means that another 1,732,684 individuals would need to be tested. Based on our model, this sequence of testing can be repeated after one, two, four, and eight weeks to reduce the prevalence of the disease to zero. However, the number of individuals to be tested in each round will be higher in subsequent rounds. In this scenario, 7,168,422 individuals will need to be tested in total. The cost of testing in Zambia is US$20 per test. Based on the assumptions made in this study, the total cost of testing would be US$143,480,440. This money could be used to provide 2,271 ventilators (at a cost of US$63,000 each) that may be needed during the COVID-19 epidemic in Zambia. samples.ref: Ukujwayelekelisa okuphansi kwamaphuzu enxubefuzo kubantu base-Afrika ngenxa yokuhlukahluka kofuzo kanye nemvelo
samples.hyp:
The recent advances in polygenic scores (PGS) have sparked a lot of interest in the field of complex trait genetics. However, most of the research on PGS has been conducted in European populations. Therefore, it remains unclear to what extent the low generalizability of PGS observed in European vs. African genetic variants is due to differences in the polygenic architecture of these populations or to the heterogeneity of the reference sets used to train the PGS models. To disentangle these two factors, we performed a meta-analysis of published PGS studies for five complex traits (height, education, schizophrenia, intelligence, and lifespan) in seven African populations. We then compared the generalizability of PGS across these populations with that of PGS for the same traits in European populations. Our results suggest that the low generalizability of PGS observed in African populations is largely driven by the heterogeneity of the reference sets used to train the PGS models rather than by the unique polygenic architecture of these populations.

samples.hyp:
The genetic underpinnings of many common diseases have been identified in people of European ancestry. But do these findings generalize to other populations? New work shows that, when it comes to genetic predictors of disease, the answer is often no.

African Ancestry

People of African ancestry have a unique genetic history that can complicate predictions of genetic risk of disease.

New research published in Genome Medicine estimates that only 85% of genetic predictors of disease in people of European ancestry are also applicable to people of African ancestry. The work also shows that studies of people of African ancestry have been significantly underpowered to date, and thus not sufficiently robust to predict genetic risk of disease in this population.

“Genetic risk scores are used to make predictions about disease risk in people who do not yet have the disease,” says Ela Kardia, professor and director of the Center for Genomic Medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. “But these scores are based on data from people of European ancestry, and it’s unclear how well they predict risk in people of African ancestry.

“This study shows that these scores are not generalizable to people of African ancestry, and that studies in people of African ancestry yield null results not because the effect is truly zero, but because the studies lack power to detect a small effect.”

Kardia, who was not involved with the new work, added that the findings underscore the importance of studying populations in their own right, and not just as a way to apply knowledge generated in other groups.

Precision medicine

The new work was conducted by researchers at the University of Washington and the University of Cape Town, and used genetic data from the African Diaspora Study, a resource that aggregates information from 150 studies involving people of African ancestry from around the world.

The researchers focused on 40 common diseases, and compared the performance of genetic predictors in people of European ancestry with that of people of African ancestry. They found that, for the most part, genetic risk scores for European ancestry do not reproduce in people of African ancestry.

“The results are not all that surprising to me,” says Terumasa Aoki, a bioinformatician at the University of Washington in Seattle and the first author on the new paper. “My intuition told me that these predictions would not transfer. But it’s important to actually carry out the work to establish it.”

The PRS is a number representing the probability that an individual will have a particular disease, based on the combined effect of multiple genetic variants that contribute to the disease in an additive manner, but do not act in an independent or synergistic manner. The variants are usually selected a priori based on their known association with disease in a (typically) large case-control study or genome-wide association study (GWAS).

The PRS has several desirable theoretical properties. First, in contrast to direct genetic testing for common disease-causing variants, the PRS can be readily calculated in an individual even if all their DNA has been destroyed e.g. used in criminal investigations. Second, the PRS has the potential to predict the risk of disease in an additive manner, even though the underlying genetic variants themselves do not act in an additive manner, by assuming that the effects of different variants are independent. Third, the PRS can be readily calculated in an individual whose genetic ancestry is mixed (e.g. a person of African and European descent), which is important given the paucity of African ancestry in available datasets.

There are some important differences between the PRS and ancestry-based risk prediction. Ancestry-based risk prediction models calculate the probability of an individual having a particular variant (e.g. West African ancestry) and the effect size of that variant (e.g. increased risk of disease), and then multiplies them together to get an estimate of risk. The PRS, on the other hand, uses multiple genetic variants as predictors, and therefore does not require the effect sizes of the variants to be the same (since they are assumed to act additively). This is a key reason why the PRS can be calculated in individuals with mixed ancestry, since the effect sizes of variants associated with different ancestral components usually are different. Across sub-Saharan Africa, the burden and trends of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), congenital anomalies (CAs) and other conditions are not well described, especially at the local district level. NTDs in particular are easy to overlook because they are often associated with poverty and tend to affect the poorest, most isolated and most marginalized communities. Yet NTDs are among the leading causes of acquired disability worldwide, while CAs can have a profound effect on affected individuals, families and communities. In 2016, the World Health Organization estimated that 270 million people worldwide required treatment for NTDs; among these, 40 million children were in need of interventions for soil-transmitted helminthiases and 17 million for lymphatic filariasis. In 2018, an estimated 17 million people worldwide required treatment for onchocerciasis; 22 million for schistosomiasis; 12 million for trichiasis; 900,000 for river blindness; and 240,000 for loiasis. In 2019, 17.5 million people in Africa required preventive chemotherapy for malaria. In 2018, 303,000 babies were born with Down syndrome in Africa, and 270,000 with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), 75,000 with spina bifida and 55,000 with clubfoot. Yet, for many of these conditions, treatment and care are available but not reaching the people who need them most. In addition, the burden of poly-morbidity and co-morbidity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) including Africa is rising, yet the capacity to manage these conditions is limited. The aim of this study was to assess the prevalence of six NTDs, four CAs and three other conditions in a district in Kenya and to explore associations between these conditions and socio-demographic characteristics of affected individuals.

samples.ref: Ukuhlolwa Kokuhlolwa Okubonwayo kanye Ne-Cytology Screening Ekuvimbeleni I-Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia kanye Nomdlavuza Womlomo wesibeletho e-Namibia
samples.hyp:
This study evaluated the performance of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) with or without human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, and cervical cytology for cervical screening in Namibia, a setting with resource constraints and high prevalence of HIV and cervical cancer.
Nineteen screening sites entered 23, 637 women aged 30-69 years. Trained providers performed VIA, cervical cytology, and HPV testing in conjunction with cervical cancer education and referred women with abnormal results for diagnostic colonoscopy. Among 20, 579 women (95.8%) with both VIA and cervical cytology results, 1, 744 (8.5%) had an abnormal cytology result and/or VIA result. Of these, 1, 069 (61.4%) had a normal HPV test result and 675 (38.6%) had an unknown or positive HPV result; the majority, 604 (89.1%), of women with an unknown or positive HPV result were aged ≥50 years. Among 17, 133 (84.3%) women with both VIA and HPV test results, 764 (4.5%) had an abnormal HPV result and/or VIA result. Of these, 227 (29.7%) had an abnormal cytology result. The percentage of women with an abnormal cytology result who also had an abnormal VIA result declined with increasing age (P for trend <0.001). Concomitant performance of VIA and HPV testing identified a population of older women who were HPV negative and VIA positive.
VIA in conjunction with cytology or HPV testing identified women with premalignant lesions and early cervical cancer who would have been missed when either test was performed alone. Given the low socioeconomic resources in Namibia, the high prevalence of HIV, the high frequency of the HPV 16/18 oncogenic types, and the advanced stage at which the majority of cervical cancers are diagnosed, the combined use of VIA and HPV testing is recommended for cervical cancer screening in this setting.

We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection of the cervix with acetic acid (VIA), and visual inspection of the cervix with potassium hydroxide (KOH) for cervical pre-cancerous lesions management in a resource-limited setting. We searched for randomised controlled trials, clinical effectiveness studies, cost-effectiveness studies and studies reporting disease progression from cervical pre-cancerous lesions in Medline, Embase, Cinahl, Global Health, PanguP, African Journals Online, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from January 1980 to August 2017. We included studies reporting on the management of cervical pre-cancerous lesions in women without symptoms. Two reviewers independently screened and selected studies for inclusion, appraised risk of bias, and extracted data. For the economic evaluation, we included also modelling studies. Meta-analysis was performed for both the clinical and economic evaluation. From seven trials including 21,144 women, we did not identify any trial that evaluated HPV testing in combination with VIA or KOH. VIA with immediate tissue biopsy for positive results and no additional cytology than the index sample for negative results was the most effective strategy for the management of cervical pre-cancerous lesions with a cancer incidence rate of 7.2 per 1000 woman-years (95% CI 4.5 to 10.9 per 1000 woman-years). However, it was not cost-effective with a high incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $US 10,607.02 (95% CI $US 7552.70 to $US 26,349.37) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained compared with best practice. The cost-effectiveness of other strategies was even worse. Summary of evidence showed that women with positive VIA or KOH would significantly benefit from repeat VIA or KOH and referral for colposcopy for those with persisting lesions. There is a lack of evidence from randomized controlled trials on the comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of strategies combining HPV testing and VIA or KOH. VIA with immediate tissue biopsy for positive results and no additional cytology than the index sample for negative results was the most effective strategy for the management of cervical pre-cancerous lesions but not cost-effective.

The aim of this study was to examine the association between age and SCC of the cervix in women with and without HIV. A retrospective cohort study was conducted of women diagnosed with SCC of the cervix between 2000 and 2014 at a tertiary hospital in Johannesburg. Inclusion criteria were age ≥16 years and a histological diagnosis of SCC of the cervix. Women with a history of cervical pre-cancer or cancer were included. Exclusion criteria were absence of a biopsy report and incomplete mycoplasmal and HPV status. Staging was not performed. Demographic, clinical and laboratory data were extracted from the medical records. The study population included 161 women with HIV and 277 HIV-negative women. The median age of the cohort was 56 years (IQR 43–66). The HIV-positive women were older (median age 57 years vs. 52 years, p<0.0001) and significantly more likely to be of black race (p=0.01) and have a CD4 count <200 cells/μL (p<0.001). HIV status was known to 68% of women diagnosed with SCC of the cervix in 2000 (n=7), increasing to 93% in 2014 (n=212). A higher proportion of HIV-positive women presented at an advanced stage of disease (p=0.03). HIV-positive women were significantly more likely to be diagnosed with SCC of the uterine cervix vs. vagina or vulva (OR 2.58, 95% CI 1.47–4.51, p=0.002). In HIV-positive women, the risk of SCC of the cervix increased with age (p=0.03). In HIV-negative women, no significant association between age and site of SCC was found (p=0.56). After adjusting for CD4 count, the association between age and cervical SCC still remained significant in HIV-positive women (p=0.02). The majority of women presented with advanced stage disease, regardless of HIV status. However, HIV-positive women were diagnosed at an advanced stage significantly more often. In women with HIV, the risk of SCC of the cervix increased with age; this association was not found in HIV-negative women. The association between age and cervical SCC was independent of CD4 count in women with HIV.

HPV testing is an important component of cervical cancer prevention and should be used as a screening method either alone or in combination with the Pap test. Women age 30 and older should be screened using HPV testing alone every 5 years. Screening for CIN 2/3 and cancer using HPV testing in women age 30 and older is as effective as Pap testing in women age 20-29. Primary screening with HPV testing is preferred over Pap testing for women age 30 and older due to the better accuracy and ease of testing, decreased frequency of screening, and reduced risk of false positive Pap test results. If the initial HPV test result is negative, no further HPV testing is needed for that 5-year period. If the initial result is positive, further management and frequency of testing will depend on a woman’s age and other risk factors. For women age 30 and older, colposcopy and cervical biopsy may be used as the initial test for HPV-positive women and colposcopy only for repeat testing. For women age 20-29, Pap testing is still the preferred initial test; repeat testing will depend on the initial Pap result. For women who have been diagnosed with a high-risk HPV infection but have no abnormal cervical cell findings on Pap testing, no further screening is needed until the same age group recommendations apply. For women who are HIV positive, screening should begin at age 25. For women at high risk for cervical cancer due to an autoimmune disease, it is unclear what age to start screening.

The study found that human papillomavirus (HPV) testing and cervical cancer screening should start at age 30 instead of 35, and pre-treatment for cervical disease should occur at age 25 instead of 30.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and other international health agencies recommend that cervical cancer prevention programs begin cervical cancer screening and HPV testing in women aged 25-65 years. However, little is known about the optimal ages for these interventions in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), which are disproportionately affected by cervical cancer.
To address this question, Nguva Shoko and colleagues used data from 3,446 women aged 15-44 years who participated in two rounds of the Namibia Population-based HPV (NAPHAP) study, a population-based survey of HPV infection and cervical disease in Namibia. The researchers examined the risks of cervical cancer and precancerous lesions by age at screening and found that the risks increased significantly as women got older. They used a mathematical model to estimate the benefits, harms, and costs of three cervical cancer screening strategies for women aged 30-44 years. The strategies were: HPV testing only, visual inspection of the cervix with human papillomavirus testing for women with positive results (known as HPV testing referral strategy), and visual inspection of the cervix followed by treatment for cervical disease (known as treat-referral strategy). The researchers compared the outcomes of these strategies to a "do nothing" strategy, which involved no screening, and found that all three strategies had far fewer cases of cervical cancer or precancerous lesions than the do nothing strategy. However, they found that the HPV testing referral strategy was more effective than the other strategies and resulted in the fewest deaths.
According to the WHO, cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women globally, causing approximately 570,000 deaths each year. The organization estimates that 85% of these deaths occur in LMICs.
The study was conducted by researchers from the University of New Mexico, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Ministry of Health and Population of Namibia.

Authors: de Villiers A, Kohli SS, Kohli AK, Dickson R, Blackard WG, Tell LA, Kew C, Kapil M, Lok ASB
We compared the frequency of HIV-1 drug resistance mutations (BamH1 polymorphism) and HBV genotypes in South African patients with HBV/HIV coinfection (n = 99) and HBV monoinfection (n = 104) who failed anti-HBV therapy with entecavir or tenofovir. Patients with coinfection were treated with cobicistat-boosted protease inhibitors. HBV genotypes were determined by PCR and sequencing. Patients with coinfection had significantly higher frequencies of the M184V mutation (coinfection 24%, monoinfection 14%, p = 0.02) associated with reduced entecavir and tenofovir susceptibility. There was a trend for increasing HBV genotypes B and C and decreasing genotypes A and E in HBV/HIV coinfection compared to HBV monoinfection. Seventy-nine patients (79%) were treated with cobicistat-boosted atazanavir, ritonavir, darunavir or lopinavir. Four (5%) developed steady state serum trough concentrations of cobicistat and/or protease inhibitor exceeding 1μM which can potentially select for resistance. In conclusion, HBV/HIV coinfection is characterized by a higher frequency of the entecavir/tenofovir resistance mutation and a shift in HBV genotype distribution. The majority of patients were safely treated with cobicistat-boosted protease inhibitors.

samples.hyp:
in Africa

The study, published in the Journal of Hepatology, suggests that healthcare providers in Africa should test patients’ anti-viral drug levels to ensure high levels and minimal side effects.

Hepatitis B is a liver disease that affects 257 million people worldwide. Although it is vaccine-preventable and treatable, it remains a major global health issue. While effective therapies have been available for over 20 years, many patients in resource-constrained settings have limited access to these treatments.

Led by Dr. Manos Paraskevakos from the University of Bern in Switzerland, the research team analyzed data from 419 patients with advanced hepatitis B, treated with the multi-drug regimen tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine for at least one year.

The team found that healthcare providers had to manage many challenges to optimize treatment outcomes. These included long hospital distances, frequent stock-outs of anti-viral drugs, limited access to laboratory tests, and a shortage of trained healthcare staff.

Fiona Murphy, Professor of Global Health at the University of Edinburgh, said: “This study highlights the need for personalized medicine approaches in resource constrained settings. By measuring drug levels and liver injury biomarkers, healthcare providers are able to ensure that patients receive the right dose at the right time and avoid treatment failure.”

The study also highlighted the importance of further research in this area. Professor Chris Bouchard, from the University of California Los Angeles, added: “Future studies should focus on implementing and evaluating simplified and potentially more accessible treatment regimens in resource-constrained settings in Africa.”

Dr. Paraskevakos is now working towards implementing these findings in clinical practice in Africa. He is founding member of the African Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and plays an active role in developing guidelines for hepatitis care in Africa.

The HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) is typically used as a marker to determine the success of antiviral treatment since it is one of the last proteins expressed before HBV is cleared from the body. In patients co-infected with HBV and HIV, the HBsAg clearance rate is lower and the time taken for its clearance is longer compared to patients only infected with HBV. It has, however, been difficult to distinguish between the effects of HBV and HIV on HBsAg clearance in co-infected patients since a suitable animal model is not available.

To overcome this issue, researchers from the University of New Mexico used a mouse model expressing human leukocyte antigen A*0201 to mimic HBV and HIV co-infection. Mice were infected with HBV alone or with a combination of HBV and HIV. The researchers then treated the mice with interferon-alpha, an antiviral protein that is currently used to treat patients with HBV. The results of the study indicated that mice infected with both HBV and HIV cleared HBsAg more quickly and with a higher rate than mice infected with HBV alone.

The researchers also found that the rate of HBsAg clearance was slower in mice infected with HBV and HIV compared to mice only infected with HIV. This suggests that HBV infection may influence the kinetics of HBsAg clearance during HBV/HIV co-infection. The researchers, however, noted that the mice used in the study were not infected with a low HBV load since the HBV infection was introduced to the mice via their drinking water. It is possible that the results may not be the same if the mice had been infected with a low HBV viral load.

The study was the first to use a mouse model to compare the kinetics of HBsAg clearance in mice infected with HBV alone or with a combination of HBV and HIV after treatment with interferon-alpha. Although further research is required, the study provides new insight into the kinetics of HBsAg clearance in patients co-infected with HBV and HIV.

The study was published in the Journal of Entrepreneurship and Small Business Management, published by the Academy of Entrepreneurship.

Abstract
Background
Spontaneous preterm birth is a leading cause of perinatal mortality and morbidity worldwide. The risk for preterm birth is increasing in many parts of the world. Malnutrition is a known risk factor for preterm birth, however it is not clear which nutrients are of importance.
Objectives
To examine the association between serum concentrations of selected trace elements (selenium, copper and zinc) and risk of spontaneous preterm birth.
Design and setting
A case-control study was conducted in three countries in Africa (Malawi, South Africa and Tanzania) with low socioeconomic status. A total of 216 women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth (< 37 gestational weeks) and 368 controls (women with birth after ≥ 37 gestational weeks) participated in the study. All participants answered a questionnaire and had blood taken for trace element analysis.
Results
Crude odds ratios (OR) for preterm birth in relation to quartiles of selenium, copper and zinc concentrations in maternal serum were consistently elevated for all countries and for all three elements, although not for the highest quartile of zinc concentrations. A total of 118 women with singletons and 62 with twins were included in the analysis. Maternal serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured in maternal serum in early pregnancy. The odds of preterm birth were higher for women with low concentrations of selenium (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.22–3.56, p = 0.008) and copper (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.03–3.05, p = 0.04). A reduced odds of preterm birth were observed for women with high concentrations of zinc (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.04–0.92, p = 0.04) and selenium (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21–0.68, p = 0.002). No association between serum concentrations of zinc and preterm birth were found. The odds of preterm birth were also higher for women with a high concentration of copper and low concentration of selenium (OR 3.95, 95% CI 1.44–10.84, p = 0.008). Our results suggest that low concentrations of selenium and copper, and high concentrations of zinc in maternal serum may increase the risk of preterm birth.

The objective of this study was to determine the concentration of selenium, copper, and zinc in pregnant women and to evaluate the relationship between these elements and gestational age. This is a prospective observational study. It included all pregnant women referring to Imam Reza medical facility for pregnancy complications from January 2018 to January 2019. After collecting 5 ml of the blood of each participant, the serum was separated from the blood samples and stored at -20°C. The concentration of copper, zinc, and selenium was measured using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer. The correlation of these elements with gestational age was evaluated using the Spearman test. P<0.05 was considered significant. This study was conducted on 70 pregnant women in the first trimester and continued until the delivery, with the mean age of 26.1±5.2 years. The mean gestational age was 38.0±1.5 weeks. The mean concentration of copper, selenium, and zinc in the first trimester of pregnancy was 15.1±5.0 mcg/dl, 113.6±10.9 mcg/dl, and 24.2±6.1 mcg/dl, respectively. There was a significant negative correlation between copper and gestational age (r=-0.34, P=0.01) and a significant positive correlation between selenium and gestational age (r=0.24, P=0.03). No significant correlation was found between the concentration of zinc and gestational age (P=0.1). There was no deficiency of zinc and selenium in the subjects, but 12.9% of them had high serum copper concentrations (>19 mcg/dl). High serum copper concentrations in pregnancy may be related to pre-eclampsia and low birth weight.

Selenium; Zinc; Copper; Pregnancy

Background: Selenium (Se), copper (Cu), and zinc (Zn) are essential micronutrients required for proper immune system function, and deficiencies have been associated with an increased risk of preterm birth (PTB). However, the relationship between PTB and Se, Cu, and Zn status is unclear.

Objectives: The purpose of this review was to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of the associations between PTB and Se, Cu, and Zn and to identify potential sources of heterogeneity in the literature.

Design: This is a priori-defined systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies of PTB in association with Se, Cu, and Zn.

Setting: Community and hospital settings.

Participants: This review included studies of pregnant women that evaluated Se, Cu, or Zn and PTB, published between January 1, 1980, and August 31, 2018.

Interventions: Intervention studies were excluded.

The researchers also found that the women who had the highest concentrations of selenium had a higher risk of delivering preterm. The study was conducted at the Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg, in collaboration with Chalmers University of Technology and the University Hospital in Örebro.

The study included 43 women who had preterm births and 79 women who had given birth at term. The women answered a food questionnaire and blood samples were collected soon after they gave birth. The researchers then analyzed the risk of preterm birth in relation to the concentrations of selenium, copper and zinc in the blood.

The results showed a clear link between high concentrations of selenium and an increased risk of delivering preterm. The risk of preterm birth increased by 60 percent for those in the top 10 percent for selenium. The other micronutrients were not associated with the risk of preterm birth.

Previous studies have shown that high concentrations of selenium may have a toxic effect on the early embryo. Other studies have shown that selenium is essential for the development of the placenta and the immune system of the expectant mother.

Selenium is a trace element that is found in small quantities in soil and is absorbed by plants and passes on to animals and humans. It is therefore found in food of both animal and plant origin. Fish, offal, wholegrain products, legumes and nuts are particularly rich in selenium. Selenium is also added to some types of salt.

Cecilia Lundqvist, PhD student at the Department of Clinical and Experimental Medicine, is the main author of the study.

“Our previous studies have shown that the concentration of selenium is higher among women who have given birth prematurely, compared with women who have given birth at term. Maternal plasma was collected at 12–14 weeks’ gestation and assayed for 15 nutrients, namely: vitamin D, vitamin A, folate, ferritin, vitamin E, selenium, potassium, calcium, copper, iron, vitamin C, beta-carotene, zinc, long-chain n-3 fatty acids and 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Compared with the controls, the cases had a higher concentration of copper (p = 0.003), and lower concentrations of E (p = 0.003), folate (p = 0.03), and Zn (p = 0.01). There was no difference between the two groups with respect to the other 11 nutrients. When the micronutrients were compared in combination, the cases had higher ratios of Cu/E (p = 0.002) and Cu/Zn (p = 0.01), and a lower ratio of E/Zn (p = 0.01). There was no difference between the two groups with respect to the ratios of D/25(OH)2D (p = 0.32), Se/Zn (p = 0.34), and n-3/total fatty acids (p = 0.35). Our results suggest that an imbalance in the micronutrients Cu, E, folate, and Zn may play a role in the etiology of preterm birth. The results show that low blood levels of selenium, copper and zinc are associated with smaller head circumference of the baby, low levels of selenium and zinc are associated with a lower body weight of the baby and low levels of selenium, copper and zinc are associated with an earlier birth.

Dr. Cees de Jonge, researcher at Wageningen University & Research: “These results are important for the many pregnant women in Malawi and other East African countries. It is likely that other pregnant women in other low-income countries, such as India and Indonesia, have similar needs. In the coming years, we will investigate whether a multiple micronutrient supplementation is effective and well-tolerated by pregnant women in Malawi.”

Dr. de Jonge elaborates on the significance of the results: “We found that about 40% of the pregnant women had a low blood level of selenium, 15% had a low blood level of copper and 1.5% had a low blood level of zinc. These micronutrients are essential for the development of the baby. Our results suggest that severe deficiency is not common, but that subtle deficiencies, which you can only measure with a blood test, are present in a large part of the population. For the selenium and copper deficiency, our findings are in line with other studies that we and others have conducted in other parts of the world. This is the first time that zinc deficiency is measured in Malawi. Earlier, we have only measured zinc deficiency in India and Indonesia.”

The study was conducted in Malawi in collaboration with the University of Malawi, University of Southampton, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, and Queen Mary University of London. The research team went to different locations in Malawi where they did a population-based study among 839 pregnant women between 12 and 27 weeks of pregnancy to measure the effect of the combination of selenium, copper and zinc. They went to the homes of the women to take blood and urine samples, measure the size of the abdomen and take height measurements of the babies. After three months, both the mother and the baby were measured again. In total, 736 women completed the study.

The researchers used a so-called randomisation technique in which lotteries were drawn for the women to determine which women received the micronutrient combination and which women received a placebo. samples.ref: Ukuziphatha Kwasekhaya, Ukwethembeka Kwesayithi kanye Nendawo yofudu lwePancake (Malacochersus tornieri) eKenya
samples.hyp:
Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya

The Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) is the second most popular tortoise in the pet trade after the Indian Star tortoise (Geochelone elegans). This species is also sought after for human consumption. The species is listed on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and in Annex A of the Washington Convention (CITES, 1995a; CITES, 1995b). Although the species is listed, it is still legally traded. Trade in M. tornieri is thought to be primarily for the pet trade (Stebbins, 1995), but live animals have also been reported as food in some areas (Bour, 1984; Georgiadis, 1989). The species is endemic to the dry areas of Kenya, where it occurs in a number of protected areas (Georgiadis, 1989; JT Jones pers. obs.). There are also substantial numbers of the species on private land (JT Jones pers. obs.). Although the species occurs in a number of protected areas, little is known about the ecology of the species. This is surprising as the species is popular in the pet trade and as food. This is particularly surprising as the species has a relatively long life span (up to 100 years) (JT Jones and GJ Blamires pers. obs.), which would allow the population to decline substantially before reaching the point of threatened status. The aim of this study was to examine aspects of the ecology of the Pancake tortoise in Kenya. In particular, the study examined aspects of the homing ability, site fidelity and territoriality of the species.

Georgiadis, N. K. (1995). The Pancake Tortoise, Malacochersus tornieri, in Kenya. In: A. C. H. Vincent (ed.), Reproduction of Tortoises and Freshwater Turtles, pp. 101–106. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

samples.hyp:
The ability of animals to navigate through their environment is a complex trait that relies on a combination of sensory cues, cognitive processes, and heritable factors. In the present review, we summarize recent findings regarding the molecular and neural mechanisms underlying spatial and temporal behaviors in two model systems: the monogamous prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster) and the social bee (Apis mellifera). We discuss how neurochemical systems, particularly those involving oxytocin and classical neurotransmitters, contribute to the development and expression of species-typical temporal and spatial behaviors in these organisms. Oxytocin plays a role in the formation of social bonds and mother-infant interactions in voles as well as the formation of dance patterns in honey bees. In both of these species, oxytocin is involved in the consolidation of long-term memory, a process which is also influenced by exposure to classical neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin. An improved understanding of the molecular underpinnings of temporal and spatial behaviors will yield valuable insights into not only normal animal behavior but also animal disorders of neuropsychiatric diseases that may be relevant to human conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, social anxiety, and addiction.

samples.ref: Ukuqonda ukuziphatha okunjalo kuyisinyathelo esibalulekile ekulondolozweni nasekulawuleni ngempumelelo ikakhulukazi izilwane ezisengozini.
samples.hyp:
Here, we study the role of religion and culture in the perception and conservation of the greater one-horned rhinoceros, a species at the brink of extinction. We focus on a state in northeastern India, Assam, which has the highest rhinoceros density in the world and is home to more than 80% of the species' global population. We use a combination of surveys and semi-structured interviews with key informants to understand how local people perceive the species and its conservation. We find that local people have a very close emotional connection with the species and consider it an integral part of their culture and religious beliefs. This close connection, however, also reveals underlying challenges to the species's conservation. For instance, many people consider the species sacred and believe that disturbing it might anger deities and lead to disasters. These people, therefore, do not support rhinoceros conservation efforts that require reducing its habitat or restricting human access to its core areas. We find that the local people's connection to the species can either facilitate or hinder conservation actions. Hence, it is crucial to (i) better understand the local people's connection to the species and (ii) design conservation programs that tap into and build upon this connection to achieve the best conservation outcomes. Our study provides a framework for other conservation practitioners to understand the local community's connection to other threatened species and design effective conservation programs.

The study area was in Mwingi West Constituency, Mwingi South Sub-County, Kitui County, Kenya. The study site was along the Chuka-Mwingi road, 2 km North of Mwingi Town and 500 m off the Chuka-Mwingi road. The area lies between latitudes 0° 43′ 42.52″ and 0° 44′ 32.59″ North of the Equator and longitudes 37° 40′ 41.52″ and 37° 42′ 19.70″ East of the Prime Meridian. The topography of the area is generally flat with patches of rocky outcrops and undulating terrain. The geology of the area is comprised of volcanic rocks of the Tertiary age (Kenyatta et al., 2010). The volcanic rocks are composed of alkaline igneous rocks, predominantly phonolites with felsic and alkaline intrusions of granites, syenites, and nephelines. The soils of the area are of basaltic origin, deep, and well-drained (NFC, 2008). The climate of the area is generally hot and dry with a single rainy season. The long rains start in March and end in May while the short rains start in October and end in December. The average annual rainfall is 700 mm (NFC, 2008). The study site is within the semi-arid agro-ecological zone of Kenya. The vegetation of the area is characterised by open woodlands with a tree density of 120 trees/ha and a grass layer cover of 50% (NFC, 2008). The trees in the area are mainly Dominica enset (Ensete ventricosum), Vungu (Milicia excelsa), Minga (Hildebrandtia abyssinica), and River paper-bark (Celtis dubia). The grass species are Kikuyu (Pennisetum clandestinum), Rhodes (Chloris gayana), Setaria (Setaria zeoaglyphoides), and Elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum). The study site is bordered to the North by public farmland, to the East by a seasonal river (Mwingi River), to the South and West by private farmland.

The study site is located in the South Indian state of Tamil Nadu. Mean body mass of the tortoises was 55.5 kg, and the home range size was 3.5 ha. The tortoises utilized the core area within their home range more than the peripheral areas. The utilization distribution of the study site was multimodal with four major use areas of the tortoises. The utilization distribution of the study site was stable from year to year. The tortoises were most active in the morning and evening, and the active time was 4.2 h per day. The tortoises spent 73.1% of their time in the open (outside the crevices) and 26.9% in the crevices. The tortoises moved between the crevices and open areas throughout the year, but the movement was less between March and May owing to high ambient temperatures. The tortoises used a variety of postures while moving in the open: walking, stepping, stretching, sitting, standing, basking, and defecating. In crevices, they used resting, standing, and basking postures. The tortoises were mainly solitary, but up to four individuals shared a crevice. The home range of male tortoises (3.8 ha) was slightly smaller than that of female tortoises (4.3 ha). The number of individuals per crevice did not affect the home range size. However, the home range size increased with body mass of the tortoises. The tortoises did not show a preference for a particular crevice. All the crevices were used throughout the year. The number of crevices used by the tortoises was not affected by sex, body mass, carapace length, or the number of individuals. But, the number of crevices used by the tortoises increased with age. The tortoises moved between the crevices and open areas throughout the year. The tortoises used the crevices as a retreat when it rained. During the southwest monsoon, the tortoises moved up to 1,366 m away from their home range to feed. The tortoises fed on 14 plant species from eight plant families, and fruit was their preferred food. The results suggest that the tortoises maintain a large home range and move between the crevices and open areas to exploit the abundant food resources in the study site.

Fourteen of the tortoises were fitted with radio-transmitters and trans-located from their respective home crevices to other crevices away from their respective home crevices and their movement and behavior monitored. The results showed that the tortoises held in captivity were under a lot of stress and that stress was reflected in their blood parameters, the quality of their shells and their behavior. The study also showed that the trans-located tortoises moved very little after trans-location. They were also shown to return to their original home crevice. This study is the first of its kind in the Transkei and would assist in the conservation of these endangered species. It is also the first study to monitor the movement and behavior of these tortoises after trans-location.

However, there was a statistically significant difference between the numbers of tortoises present in the crevices and the numbers of tortoises in the surrounding area (t = −4.88, P <0.0001). This finding suggests that the surrounding area is an important factor limiting the number of tortoises that can use a particular beach. The number of tortoises present in the crevices was not correlated with the amount of available burrow space (Spearman r = 0.132, P > 0.05). This suggests that other factors such as the availability of food, which was not investigated here, may be important in limiting the number of tortoises present in the crevices. The number of tortoises present in the crevices was negatively correlated with the percentage of open burrows (Spearman r = −0.233, P <0.05). Pancake tortoises are masterful navigators. (© Alex Bond)

It’s not yet 8am, but the temperature is already beginning to soar. I’m in the Namib Desert with a group of researchers investigating the movements of the enigmatic pancake tortoise. This elusive creature is only found in the dry sand dunes of the Namib and Kaokoveld, a vast area spanning much of south-western Angola and southern Namibia.

We climb to the top of a dune, waiting for our guide to catch up. He has the rather unenviable task of navigating down the other side, something of a challenge when the gradient is almost vertical. The pancake tortoise is well adapted to its arid habitat. It digs a burrow in which to escape the scorching heat and which provides refuge from predators. In fact, this tortoise only emerges from its burrow after several days of heavy rainfall, when the ground is soft enough to allow it to dig in its preferred direction — that is, downhill.

The pancake tortoise is one of the longest living tortoises, with ages of over 200 years not uncommon. With such a slow rate of movement and metabolism, it’s hard to imagine they disperse at all. Yet, occasionally, when its population numbers drop, researchers have observed them climbing dunes they would not normally climb, risking the hot sun to move from dune to dune, and even, on at least one occasion, crossing the road and entering a new area.

We wait for our guide, gazing out over the vast expanse of the Namib, an area that is the only place in the world where the pancake tortoise can be found. It’s a breathtaking view: of rolling orange dunes, some small, some large, and in the distance, the Atlantic Ocean. It’s hard to imagine that beneath the sand there are entire communities of pancake tortoises, hiding in their burrows, waiting for the rains to return.

As we look out over this landscape, our guide suddenly appears. He has been following a radio-tracked individual and has heard movement in the dune directly in front of us. We begin to make our way down, slowly at first, using our feet to create a track for our descent. The study, led by the University of Helsinki, shows that the animals have a remarkable ability to determine their position in relation to the sun, the stars, and the landscape. The study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

The East African pancake tortoise is a rare species endemic to Kenya and northern Tanzania. The shell of the adult tortoise is not more than 15 centimetres long. The small size and unusual appearance of the pancake tortoise have contributed to it being one of the most understudied turtle species in the world, despite being classified as a critically endangered species.

"We knew that the tortoises have a pretty good sense of direction, but we were still surprised to discover that they are able to find their way back to their home range after being released far away, possibly due to their strong homing instinct," says the first author of the study, Antti Ylönen from the University of Helsinki and the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The researchers captured 31 tortoises in different locations in northern Kenya and transported them to three different release sites located more than 500 kilometres away from the capture sites. Ten of the released animals were fitted with satellite transmitters, which were used to track their movements.

The results showed that two of the released animals were unable to return to their capture sites. Of the remaining 29 animals, seven had returned to their capture sites after three months, and 11 more had returned to their capture sites after five months. The movement of the animals was restricted during the first weeks after release, but they started moving more freely on the landscape after that.

The researchers also found that the animals use a variety of different methods to find their way home. At least some of the returning animals had moved towards the sky where the sun sets, which would have given them a hint about the general direction to their home. The animals also used familiar landmarks and large landscape features, such as mountains and rivers, to guide their way home.

"The animals' ability to find their way home over such large distances was partly based on their ability to determine the position of the sun. However, they also used other cues, such as familiar landmarks, to find their way," Ylönen explains.

The study shows that M. tornieri are able to determine their position in relation to several types of cues in their environment, and they can combine different pieces of information to find their way home.

Animals use a variety of methods to remember such locations, but a new study finds that red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) are able to recall places where they've previously buried food, even when the food has been removed and up to 6 months have passed.

To find out how well the foxes remembered the locations, researchers at the University of Cambridge and the University of Exeter placed meals in stainless steel boxes on the ground, and then buried the boxes in sand at various locations. After a delay of up to 6 months, the researchers returned the food-laden boxes to their original burial sites and attached a radio transmitter to them so that the foxes could be tracked once they sprang into action. The team's findings were published this week in the journal Animal Behaviour.

In 14 out of 21 trials, the animals returned to the exact spot where the food had originally been buried, the researchers report. And in 6 of those trials, the animals found the food immediately.

"Many animals, including humans, use caches of food to get them through the winter, so being able to remember where you buried a food cache is important," says study co-author Rosie Woodroffe from the University of Exeter. "But it's rare for studies to last for more than a few weeks, so we just didn't know whether the foxes could remember where they had buried the food for many months."

The findings suggest that the red foxes in this study had no problem remembering where they had buried food, even after a long delay. The team suspects the animals may be able to use cues from the environment, such as the type of plant they buried the food under, to help them remember.

"Being able to remember where they had cached the food would be particularly helpful in winter, when you have to dig through snow to find it," says Woodroffe.

The researchers also want to investigate how the foxes are able to find their caches again after such a long time. It's possible that the foxes have a "mental map" of their territory that allows them to remember where they have been and what they have done there. If this is the case, it would suggest that the animals have a more advanced memory than previously thought.

We investigated if lower doses given for 35 days could achieve outcomes similar to those of 10 mg/kg/day given for 44 days, using a model that combines individual patient data and data from microbiological and ultra-echo studies in Malawi.

We used a previously published model to estimate the relationship between treatment duration and time to clearance of bacilli from cerebrospinal fluid, as well as the association between bacillary load and probability of a good outcome in patients treated with 10 mg/kg/day of intravenous rifampicin for 44 days. The model was then used to simulate a 10 mg/kg/day regimen for 35 days.

In patients with a good outcome, bacilli were cleared more rapidly when given 10 mg/kg/day for 35 days than when given 10 mg/kg/day for 44 days (median 18 vs 24 days, P<0·001). A similar rate of bacillary clearance was achieved when a lower dose of 4·25 mg/kg/day was given for 35 days (median 24 days, P=0·76). Patients who received the lower dose had similar probabilities of a good outcome (93% vs 100%) and death (5% vs 3%) compared to those who received the standard dose.

In a high-burden setting where resources are limited, giving a lower dose of intravenous rifampicin for 35 days achieves outcomes similar to those of a standard 10 mg/kg/day regimen given for 44 days.

We studied 11 South African children with culture-confirmed tuberculous meningitis who received either oral or intravenous regimens of rifampicin. We measured plasma rifampicin concentrations by high-performance liquid chromatography. The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) and peak concentration (C(max)) were similar for the oral (11.3 μM·h/L, 8.3 μM) and intravenous (12.8 μM·h/L, 8.6 μM) regimens. The oral-to-intravenous AUC ratio was 0.87 (90% CI 0.79-0.95) and the C(max) ratio was 0.98 (90% CI 0.87-1.10). The intravenous regimen produced higher rifampicin exposures in all participants. The intravenous regimen resulted in greater rifampicin exposures than oral therapy in children with tuberculous meningitis.

a standard group that received 10 mg/kg/day, an intensified group that received 20 mg/kg/day, and a control group that received 45 mg/kg/day. The primary outcome was the change in CSF HIV-1 RNA concentration from baseline to week 24. Secondary outcomes included changes in CSF and plasma HIV-1 RNA and plasma CD4+ cell counts. The study was terminated early due to slow recruitment.

At baseline, mean CSF HIV-1 RNA and plasma HIV-1 RNA were 4.3 and 4.2 log10 copies/mL, respectively, in the 45 mg/kg/day group; 4.3 and 4.5 log10 copies/mL, respectively, in the 10 mg/kg/day group; and 4.2 and 4.4 log10 copies/mL, respectively, in the 20 mg/kg/day group. There were no differences between the groups in change from baseline to week 24 in CSF HIV-1 RNA (P = .34), CSF HIV-1 RNA change adjusted for confounders (P = .17), plasma HIV-1 RNA (P = .25), or plasma CD4+ cell count (P = .26). There was one serious adverse event, death, in the 10 mg/kg/day group.

In this trial, more than 10,000 copies/mL reduction in CSF HIV RNA concentration was not achieved in any of the groups at week 24. HIV replication control in the CSF was not improved by either intensified rifampicin dosing or the rifampicin standard compared with a low dose of rifampicin. Study termination due to slow recruitment precludes definitive conclusions.

Adverse events were generally mild and well tolerated; 2 (18%) in the standard group, 3 (27%) in the high-dose oral group, and 1 (10%) in the intravenous group experienced treatment-emergent adverse events. Conclusion Among children with superrefractory SE, those who received intravenous fosphenytoin had a more rapid and complete reduction in seizure frequency compared with those who received standard oral fosphenytoin or high-dose oral phenytoin. Plasma samples (1.5 mL) were collected prior to the dose (0(L)) and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 24 h (0.5-24) postdose. Plasma concentrations of PF-07321332 were quantified using a lower limit of quantitation of 2 ng/mL. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using non-compartmental methods. Cmax and Tmax were observed in plasma. The terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) was calculated by linear regression of the log concentration vs. time data set from the point of the last quantifiable plasma concentration to the point of the plasma concentration below the limit of quantification. The area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC(0-24)) was calculated using the trapezoidal rule. The elimination clearance (CL) was calculated as CL = Dose/AUC(0-24). The mean residence time (MRT) was calculated as MRT = AUMC/AUC, where AUMC is the area under the first-moment concentration-time curve. The volume of distribution (Vd) was calculated as Vd = CL/F. The maximum concentration at the brain capillary wall (Cmax,BCS) was calculated using the width (W) of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) (18), a permeability surface area (PS) of 2500 cm2, and a central compartment volume of distribution (V1) of 18.3 L as Cmax,BCS = Cmax x (PS x V1)/W.

High dose pills can be tested on HIV patients with TB meningitis

A new trial will test a six-month treatment using high-dose anti-retroviral (ARV) drugs in people with HIV and multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and TB meningitis.

The trial, called THENDO, will look at whether giving higher doses of ARVs over a six-month period will help to prevent the death of people with HIV and MDR-TB with TB meningitis.

HIV and TB are leading causes of illness and death worldwide. South Africa has the highest number of people in the world living with HIV, with MDR-TB being both a significant HIV-related and standalone cause of illness and death in the country. TB meningitis is also more common in people with HIV than those without HIV.

People with HIV and TB are treated for both illnesses, but the treatments are difficult and the illnesses tend to take a toll on the body. As a result, people with both HIV and TB often do not respond well to treatment, and develop resistance to the treatments, which hampers efforts to control these epidemics.

The study will enrol 400 Hiv-positive patients, aged 18 to 65, at the study site in KwaZulu-Natal. Patients will be screened for eligibility and those that qualify will be enrolled onto the study. Participants will be randomly allocated to one of two groups. Both groups will receive the current standard-of-care, which is a combination of four anti-retroviral drugs and treatment for their TB. In addition, patients in one group will also receive a combination of three high-dose ARVs.

The study will look at whether the addition of the high-dose ARVs will help to improve outcomes for the participants.

The trial will also look at the side effects of the high-dose ARVs and will screen for neurological side effects, given that some of these drugs can have neurological side effects.

The study is being conducted by the South African Research in Antiretroviral Treatment of HIV and TB (SARTART) group, in collaboration with the Clinical HIV Research Unit at Wits University, the University of KwaZulu-Natal and the Durban Academic Centre of the National Health Laboratory Service and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

But the capsules can be difficult to swallow, and have to be administered by mouth, which can be dangerous for very sick patients. Now, a team of researchers led by Pamela Waterman at the University of Washington has found a way to give rifampicin as an inhaled powder, which could be a much less invasive way to administer the drug to patients.

The researchers, who describe their work in a new paper published online today in PLOS Pathogens, also found that the inhaled rifampicin worked just as well as the oral capsules at killing the bacteria that cause tuberculosis meningitis. And inhaled rifampicin was much better tolerated by the patients in the study, who experienced much lower rates of side effects like nausea and vomiting.

Tuberculosis meningitis is a serious and potentially deadly disease. It affects about 70,000 to 80,000 people each year, and kills one to two million people annually. Most of these deaths are in the developing world, and occur in children because children are more susceptible to the disease and because there has not been a safe and effective way to deliver the necessary treatment to them. “Children often arrive at a health center or hospital very ill,” Waterman says. “They can be too sick to eat or drink anything. To get around this problem, the researchers turned to an old drug, rifampicin, which has been used to treat tuberculosis since the 1960s. It’s often given to tuberculosis patients in combination with other drugs, and it’s also used to treat Mycobacterium leprae, the bacteria that causes leprosy. Rifampicin is a powerful drug, but it can be hard on the liver, and some patients may stop taking it because of this. It can also cause gastrointestinal side effects like nausea and vomiting, especially when taken with other tuberculosis drugs.

The researchers suspected that these side effects were at least partly due to the fact that rifampicin is given by mouth. Previous studies have shown that when other strong antibiotics are inhaled, they have more effective and less side-effect-laden formulations than when they’re given as oral capsules. So, the researchers decided to see whether inhaled rifampicin would be an effective way to treat tuberculosis meningitis.

Heart failure is one of the most common causes of hospitalisation and is often accompanied by other diseases. It is therefore important to ensure that the medication is taken as needed without the patient having to swallow the pills. The researchers also say that the method is easy to perform and does not require expensive equipment. "The dose of the drug used in our patients has not been studied before so we did not know whether we were using too much, too little or just the right amount," he said.

"Our study shows that the standard dose of 10mg per kg of body weight is not high enough and that the capsules should be crushed up to give a higher dose.

"Although the high dose has been used in other countries it has never been tested in this way before and it is the first time it has been given as a high dose.

The study will be presented today at the Paediatric Infectious Disease Society of Australia and New Zealand annual scientific meeting in Christchurch.

Rifampicin is given to patients with TB in combination with other drugs and is administered either by mouth, in capsule form, or by intramuscular or intravenous injection.

The drug has been in use for 50 years and is given as a standard dose of 10mg per kg of body weight per day, either as a single dose or two divided doses.

But in the last 18 months, there has been evidence that a high dose of the drug, administered as 20-30mg per kg of body weight per day, may be more effective in treating patients with complicated drug-resistant TB than current standards.

Stating that the median IL-6 level was significantly higher in non-survivors (P<0.001), the researchers said that the day the patient was admitted to hospital, but before ICU admission, venous blood gases were measured in 54 patients. They found that an admission pH <7.3 was associated with a worsened prognosis (P=0.01). Of the 106 patients, 29 (27%) required admission to the ICU. These patients had a higher median IL-6 level than the patients who did not require ICU admission (P<0.001). The researchers said that the day a patient was admitted to the ICU, they measured venous blood gases, lactate and bilirubin levels in 21 patients. Low pH (<7.30), high lactate (>2.0 mmol/L) and high bilirubin (>50 µmol/L) were common and were associated with a worsened prognosis (P=0.01, P=0.01 and P=0.03 respectively).

The researchers concluded by stating: “In-hospital mortality in COVID-19 is significant. The admission plasma cytokine profile and the change in blood acid-base and lactate chemistry provide prognostic information from the time of hospital admission that may assist in clinical decision-making.”

The study will be conducted by the South African Tuberculosis Vaccine Initiative (SATVI; http://www.satvi.org) in collaboration with the University of Cape Town's Institute of Meningitis Research (http://www.meningitis.org), the University of KwaZulu-Natal, and the Research Institute for Tuberculosis and Lung Diseases in Johannesburg.

The trial will be conducted at clinics in Umlazi and at the Dr. Yusuf Dadoo (Abdulhayyun) and Princess Maud hospitals in Chatsworth. All three areas have a high prevalence of HIV and TB. The trial is expected to take five years and will involve 2400 men, women, and children with HIV-associated tuberculosis meningitis.

The current recommended dose of rifampicin is 10 mg per kg, but it has been difficult to use this dose because it is difficult to get children to take it. The dose also needs to be high to be effective. The new trial will test whether a higher dose of rifampicin, customised for each patient's weight, is safe and will be more effective in treating HIV-associated tuberculosis meningitis.

SATVI is based at the University of Cape Town's Medical School and is a partnership of South African and international research groups, including the MRC's Collaborative Programs on HIV/TB Research, KwaZulu-Natal and the University of Cape Town. The group is headed by Professor Barry Schoub, and SATVI's Director of Research is Professor Helen McShane. SATVI's aim is to develop effective tuberculosis vaccines for South Africa and sub-Saharan Africa.

samples.src: Soil fertility decline is a major constraint to crop production in sub-Saharan Africa.
samples.ref: Ukwehla kokuvunda kwenhlabathi kuyingqinamba enkulu ekukhiqizeni izitshalo e-sub-Saharan Afrika
samples.hyp:
In this study, we investigated the long-term dynamics of soil fertility and crop yields on farm fields in two agro-ecological zones of Ethiopia—Wollega and Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples Region (SNNPR).

We collected data from 168 fields that had been under crop production for ≥20 years in Wollega and SNNPR between 2014 and 2019. We used a spatial regression model [SAR + Lag] to identify fields with similar trends in soil properties and crop yields.

In both regions, we observed a decline in crop yields, and in soil properties (available phosphorus and organic carbon), although the magnitude of the decline was larger in SNNPR than in Wollega. Our findings suggest that soil fertility management is a major constraint to crop production in both Wollega and SNNPR.

The spatial structure of the soil fertility-crop yield dynamics facilitated our ability to identify fields with similar long-term trends. Our study showed that it is possible to use a spatial statistics model that incorporates spatial and temporal lag effects to analyze long-term soil-crop interactions on farms.

However, the long-term effect of combined biochar and compost applications is still little investigated. Therefore, the aim of this field study was to investigate the long-term effect of biochar and compost applications on soil physical properties, soil microbial biomass, plant growth, and nutrient uptake. A field experiment with two factors (biochar and compost) in a factorial design was conducted over a period of 5 years at two locations in Germany. At both locations, biochar was applied at rates of 0, 4.5, 9, and 13 t ha−1 and compost at rates of 0, 24, 48, and 72 t ha−1. Compost was applied only in combination with biochar. The results showed that the effect of compost on the majority of the investigated parameters was more pronounced than the effect of biochar. In general, the highest effect was found at the location “A.” The interaction of biochar and compost had a significant effect on soil physical properties, soil microbial biomass, and nutrient uptake only at location “A.” Biochar and compost applications increased soil microbial biomass after 5 years. The highest microbial biomass was found at a biochar application of 4.5 t ha−1 and compost application of 24 t ha−1 at location “A” and at a biochar application of 13 t ha−1 and compost application of 48 t ha−1 at location “B.” The highest plant yield was found at biochar and compost applications of 4.5 and 24 t ha−1, respectively, at location “A.” At location “B,” the highest plant yield was found at a biochar application of 13 t ha−1 and a compost application of 48 t ha−1. The highest nutrient uptake was found at the same treatments that led to the highest plant yield.

The use of compost and biochar for soil quality management has been reported to enhance soil carbon sequestration (Laird, 2008), soil quality (Lehmann et al., 2003), and crop productivity (Chan et al., 2007; Jeffery et al., 2014; Mukurukoma et al., 2011). The application of biochar to soil has been reported to increase soil cation exchange capacity (Yamato et al., 1995), soil microbial carbon (Jin et al., 2011), available phosphorus (Mukurukoma et al., 2011), basal soil respiration (Jin et al., 2011), and crop productivity (Jin et al., 2011; Mukurukoma et al., 2011).

samples.hyp:
English text:
Biochar and compost improve soil quality for crops
Posted on 11.05.2020

The study, led by the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, used field and laboratory experiments to determine the individual and combined effects of biochar and compost on soil properties and the growth of corn, dry beans, and lettuce. The researchers evaluated biochar and compost applications alone and in combination, at rates of 0 to 40 t/ha, in a Drayton farm field. They found that applying both biochar and compost improved soil quality, and combining the two led to greater improvements than biochar or compost alone.

The study was conducted by a team of researchers from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, the University of Minnesota, and the USDA-NRCS in Illinois.

The team’s findings will be published in a forthcoming issue of the Journal of Environmental Quality.

Soil is a non-renewable resource, and its quality is of paramount importance to soil productivity, which in turn, affects crop yield, product quality, and cash flow to the farmer. Applying organic inputs such as compost can improve soil quality and health by promoting biological activity and increasing the soil’s capacity to provide plant nutrients.

Biochar can also improve soil quality and increase soil carbon. Biochar is a solid form of organic carbon made by heating biomass in an oxygen-free environment. Biochar is created through a process known as pyrolysis, which is the thermal decomposition of organic materials in an absence of oxygen.

The pyrolysis process also produces syngas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen that can be used for energy; and bio-oil, which is a liquid form of biochar. Biochar has a much larger surface area than does raw biomass; and it is highly resistant to biological and chemical degradation. This means that once plant nutrients bind to biochar during the pyrolysis process, they are protected from leaching and are made available to plants for a longer period of time.

In this study, the researchers wanted to determine if combining biochar and compost could have a synergistic effect on soil quality. They conducted field experiments at the Drayton Farm near Tuscola, Illinois, using five different treatments: compost applied at rates of 0, 15, or 30 t/ha; biochar applied at rates of 0, 20, or 40 t/ha; and a combination of compost and biochar applied at rates of 0 to 40 t
