samples.ref: Lolu cwaningo luphenye ukuthu i-biochar, umlotha ozinze kakhulu, enekhabhoni eningi, ekhandwe nge-biomass elahliwe, ingasetshenziswa kanjani ukuthuthukisa izinga lemihlabathi e sub-Saharan Afrika.
samples.hyp:
Biochar has been shown to improve plant growth through changes in the chemical and physical properties of soils. However, little is known about the response of soil microbes to biochar. Soil microbes are crucial for soil health and biochar's effects on plant growth may be mediated through changes in the soil microbial community. This is especially important for sub-Saharan Africa where little is known about the soil microbial community and where improved soil quality is urgently needed due to extensive soil degradation. In this study, we investigated the effect of biochar on the soil microbial community, measured as changes in the bacterial community phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) profile, in two soils from sub-Saharan Africa. The first experiment investigated the effect of increasing biochar quantity (2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% by weight) and the second experiment investigated the effect of biochar produced from two different feedstocks and at two different temperatures (350 and 700°C) on the bacterial PLFA profile. Biochar had little effect on the bacterial community in the lighter soil but altered the bacterial community in the heavier soil. Changes in the bacterial community were related to changes in the relative abundance of specific fatty acids, measured as changes in PLFA profiles. The effect of biochar on the bacterial community was also related to the feedstock and the production temperature of the biochar. This study suggests that the local feedstocks and production conditions should be considered to maximize the effect of biochar on the bacterial community in sub-Saharan African soils. Despite its potential to improve soil quality, biochar could have both positive and negative effects on the soil microbial community. Future research should therefore aim to identify the factors that determine whether biochar has a positive or negative effect on the soil microbial community.

The study also found that the addition of biochar to the soil can reduce the amount of nitrogen left over from fertiliser that is washed into lakes and streams, helping to improve water quality.

The researchers added that the use of biochar can also reduce greenhouse gas emissions because it absorbs nitrous oxide, a gas that is 300 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

The study is the first to show that biochar application can have multiple benefits for the environment.

The researchers applied biochar at rates of 20 tonnes per hectare to 2.4 ha of a former pasture that had last been grazed in 2016. The site had been fenced in March 2020 so the researchers were able to compare the amount of vegetation growing in areas that were grazed by sheep and cattle in 2016 with areas that had not been grazed but received biochar, and areas that had not been grazed and received neither biochar nor any other interventions.

The study, published today in Nature Sustainability, shows that adding wood ash to the soil not only provides plants with nutrients but also improves the structure of the soil, making it easier for crops to grow.

To find out the effects of this age-old practice, researchers led by the University of Sussex and The Centre for Sustainable Ecosystems and Biosecurity at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, studied 16 long-term agricultural research sites across sub-Saharan Africa.

They found that across these 16 sites, and over 100 years of study, the use of wood ash significantly improved soil structure, compared to soils that were not amended with ash.

Soil structure refers to the physical arrangement of soil particles and how they form aggregates. Soils with beneficial structure are highly porous and structured, with a network of holes and pores that allow for healthy root growth and for water and nutrients to move through the soil.

The study sites included in the research were selected because they have long-term agricultural research trials in place. Some of the research sites, such as in South Africa and Malawi, have been studying the same set of fields for over 100 years, while others such as in Uganda and Tanzania have data stretching back 30 to 50 years.

By comparing these long-term data sets with the scientific literature, the researchers were able to look at how soil structure has changed over time, and how this change was linked to the use—or lack—of wood ash.

First author Dr. Daniel Nyabukira, from the University of Sussex's Institute of Development Studies, says: "The scientific literature and our own data both show that the use of wood ash consistently improves soil structure over time. This is because wood ash contains calcium, which reacts chemically with silicon in the soil to form a glue that holds the soil particles together, creating aggregates with lots of pore space in between.

"Importantly, these benefits build up slowly over time, so you get a cumulative effect. This is not the same as applying liming, which gives a more immediate boost to nutrient availability.

"Wood ash is a readily available and inexpensive fertiliser for smallholder farmers in the region, who can collect it for free from their surroundings. The only thing they need to be careful about is not to use too much ash, as this can have the opposite effect and actually make the soil more compact.

In the present study, we used the Swedish Nation-wide Inpatient Register to identify 21,465 patients who had been hospitalized with RA for the first time and were followed up to 20 years for the development of first-ever acute myocardial infarction (AMI), secondarily for stroke, and tertiary for heart failure (HF). We also assessed the impact of RA on the in-hospital outcomes of these events. During a median of 8.2 years of follow-up, 1,287 AMIs and 686 strokes occurred. After adjustment for age and gender, and compared to the general population, patients hospitalized for RA had a 2.2-fold increased risk of AMI and a 1.6-fold increased risk of stroke. Furthermore, patients with RA were at higher risk of HF following either AMI or stroke. While the risk for developing AMI decreased with increasing RA duration, the risk of stroke was not affected by how long RA had been present before the first hospitalization. Patients with RA were at higher risk of in-hospital death following either AMI or stroke, and this was particularly pronounced among those with more severe RA. Patients with RA were also at increased risk of in-hospital HF following AMI. These findings highlight the heightened risk of cardiovascular events in RA patients early after diagnosis, and the particularly high risk of HF following AMI or stroke. This may partly explain the reduced life expectancy observed in patients with RA.

We hypothesized that fibrin formed in the presence of citrullinated fibrinogen (Cit-FG) is more thrombogenic than native fibrin. Recombinant human Cit-FG and, for correlation, native FG were covalently biotinylated and used to generate neutravidin-fibrin microbeads. Fibrin microbeads were clotted under flow conditions in a perfusion chamber and imaged by two-photon microscopy. Compared with native FG microbeads, Cit-FG microbeads showed increased thrombus growth, gelation rates, and elastic modulus. In control experiments using noncitrullinated FG, only increases in thrombus growth and gelation rates were observed. Analyses of the fibrin network showed that citrullination results in more short/long sidearms, increased number of intersections, and a higher proportion of knots. In electrophoretic and Western blot analyses, full-length and degraded fragments of α- and γ-FG were detected in the microbeads. The relative content of γ-FG increased in Cit-FG microbeads, which also contained more degraded FG. Our data demonstrate that the increased thrombogenicity of Cit-FG is based on an altered polymerization of α- and γ-FG and the generation of more degraded fibrin(ogen) species.

samples.hyp:
This is a novel technology that measures the viscoelastic properties of blood, providing information on the rate of clot formation and strength. This method provides an overall picture of the hemostatic function of the coagulation system, including both primary hemostasis (blood vessel injury and platelet plug formation) and secondary hemostasis (coagulation factor activation and fibrin formation). The results are expressed in two indices: the clotting time (R-time) and the strength of the clot (Max amplitude). In this study, we found that the R-time and Max amplitude values were significantly lower in children with SSSP than in controls (P < 0.05). The R-time and Max amplitude values were significantly correlated with the CRP level (r = 0.603 and r = 0.501, respectively; P < 0.05). Additionally, the R-time and Max amplitude values were significantly correlated with the SSSP score (r = 0.695 and r = 0.716, respectively; P < 0.01). The R-time and Max amplitude values were significantly lower in children with high SSSP scores than in those with low SSSP scores (P < 0.05).

When a blood vessel is damaged, a complex set of chemical reactions known as the coagulation cascade triggers a series of blood-clotting reactions that finally close the wound. Inflammation changes the balance of this cascade, which can result in excessive clot formation.

This is important because blood clots are supposed to form outside the body, not inside small blood vessels in the brain, where they can cause strokes, or in the heart, where they can cause heart attacks. “You want the clot to form at the site of injury. If you get a clot in a large vessel, it’s not a big deal. But if you get a clot in a small vessel, it can be devastating,” says Soumil Chakrabarti, MD, an assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Emory University School of Medicine.

Inflammation can also cause blood clots to form in larger vessels, but in a different way that’s also damaging. When inflammation occurs, the lining of blood vessels can be damaged, and that exposes blood cells to molecules that shouldn’t be there. This can trigger a process called hypercoagulation, in which the blood forms clots that can cause heart attacks or strokes. “It’s a different mechanism, but the end result is the same—blood clots that cause heart attacks or strokes,” says Chakrabarti.

Research has shown that people with diabetes are more likely to develop blood clots, and they’re also more likely to develop infections. “Inflammation is one unifying theory for both of these processes,” says Chakrabarti. “In both cases, the individual is at risk.”

This suggests that the blood fibrin may be a useful indicator of RA, and that changes to it may be an early sign of the disease.

The researchers also found that the change in the blood fibrin structure was more pronounced in early RA patients, whose disease had been diagnosed within the last 6 weeks. As RA progresses, the body produces antibodies that attack the altered blood fibrin, restoring it to a more normal structure. This may explain why the change was not seen in long-standing disease.

The test used in this study was not sensitive enough to detect the change in all early RA patients, but further research may be able to detect the change earlier and more reliably. If fibrin could be confirmed as an early marker of RA, it might be used to monitor treatment in patients who are starting anti-rheumatic therapy. Although the test used in this study was not suitable for this purpose, a more accurate test might allow doctors to assess treatment effectiveness within months of a patient starting therapy, rather than the current average of 2 years.

"Understanding the relationship between RA and CVD is important because RA patients are at a higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke," said study author Shadman Zafar, MD, a rheumatologist at Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine in Cleveland. 

"Early recognition of patients at high risk for CVD could allow for interventions targeted to those patients that could potentially reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke," said Zafar, who also is an internal medicine physician at MetroHealth System in Cleveland.

For the study, the researchers examined medical records of 3, 694 patients, including 1, 277 with RA and 2, 417 without the disease. 

Patients were followed for a median of 28.7 years, and the researchers determined the cause of death in each case.

A total of 1, 336 deaths were considered CVD-related, including 238 cardiac deaths, 877 stroke deaths, and 221 deaths from other CVDs.

After adjusting for age, sex, and other risk factors for CVD, the researchers found that RA patients had a 58% higher risk of CVD, a 37% higher risk of stroke, and a 32% higher risk of cardiac death when compared with patients without RA.

The researchers also identified several changes in the blood that were associated with CVD in RA patients.

Compared with patients without RA, those with the disease had higher levels of several types of blood cells -- including lymphocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes -- and lower levels of hemoglobin and the albumin protein.

"RA is a disease of chronic inflammation, so we expected to find inflammation markers in the blood that are associated with CVD in RA," Zafar said. "The fact that we found such markers -- and others that we didn't expect, such as monocytes and neutrophils -- is telling."
It is still unclear exactly what these blood changes mean for patients with RA, Zafar said. "It is possible that the same biological processes that cause inflammation in RA also cause changes in the blood that are associated with CVD. Or, it's possible that the changes in the blood put patients with RA at higher risk of CVD through a different biological process."

samples.src: The present study aims to address a disconnect between science and the public in the form of a potential misalignment in the supply and demand of information known as the usability gap.
samples.ref: Lolu cwaningo lwamanje luhlose ukubhekana nokunqamula ukuxhumana phakathi kwesayensi nomphakathi ngendlela yokungahle kube nokungahleleki kahle ekuhlinzekweni nasekufuneni ulwazi olwaziwa ngokuthi igebe lokusebenziseka.
samples.hyp:
The usability gap refers to the difference between the amount of scientific information that is needed by the public to make informed decisions and the amount of information that the public actually wants. The usability gap has been identified as a significant barrier to effective science communication. Science communication refers to the process of formally educated experts in a scientific field communicating their scientific knowledge to the public. The effectiveness of science communication is important in science education, as it is believed that the public should have access to scientific information and decision-making power to create their own scientific understandings. The public is defined as people who are not formally educated in a scientific field. The usability gap is particularly problematic in the context of a pandemic, as it is important for the public to have access to scientific information in order to make informed decisions about their health and safety. However, the public may not want a lot of scientific information, and instead prefer information that is easy to understand and relevant to their everyday lives. In order to address the usability gap, scientists and communicators must work together to identify the most useful and relevant information for the public and present it in a clear and concise manner. This can be done through various means, such as press releases, social media, and interactive workshops. By closing the usability gap, scientists and communicators can help ensure that the public has the information it needs to make informed decisions about health and safety measures during a pandemic.

The study employed a qualitative approach using semi-structured interviews with key informants in the aquaculture industry (n=28). These were analyzed using an inductive, bottom-up approach.

We found that metocean information was highly valued by aquaculture stakeholders, and was perceived as critical to business decisions and risk management. However, the perceived relevance and usefulness of meteorological information from weather services was variable. In Australia, metocean information was perceived as more objective, reliable and usable than other sources, while in South Africa it was considered more subjective, less reliable and less usable. In both countries, the most commonly cited constraint to using metocean information was a lack of timely, site-specific information. Stakeholders value information that is specific to their location, and can be interpreted in the context of other information (e.g. biological, environmental, and site-specific meteorological data). There is a need for simple, reliable tools and services that meet users’ specific needs, and greater engagement with users to assess the effectiveness of existing services and to develop new services that meet users’ needs.

The project will be conducted in a partnership between the South African Weather Service (SAWS) and the South African Institute for Scientific Investigation (STRAND), and includes the following objectives:

1. To understand the perceptions of South African users of weather forecasts.
2. To understand how weather forecasts are used in South Africa.
3. To develop a forecast engagement framework for low-prevalence hazards in South Africa.

The project will be conducted in three phases:

1. Contextual analysis: qualitative data will be collected on how weather forecasts are perceived, used, and engaged with. This will inform the development of the forecast engagement framework.
2. Development of a forecast engagement framework: formative research will be conducted to understand how forecasts are currently used, and how they can be improved. The resulting framework will then be tested in Phase 3.
3. Framework testing and refinement: the forecast engagement framework will be tested in a quantitative survey. Based on the survey results the framework will be finalised.

CCA is a useful tool for investigating the extent to which a set of respondents shares a specific set of understandings. It is a qualitative approach that allows for the identification of core elements of a concept and the assessment of the extent to which these elements are shared by the respondents. CCA is based on the assumption that within a culture, there is a general consensus on the basic elements of a specific concept. In this study, the concept was the meaning of the term “peer review.” The respondents were 104 authors who had published articles in the 32 journals that publish the highest number of articles in general surgery in the United States. The authors were asked to order 48 statements that reflected their perceptions of peer review in order of importance. The degree of agreement was assessed using a model-based approach. The results show that there is a general consensus among the respondents on 8 of the 10 core elements of peer review. The elements that showed the lowest level of consensus were related to the meaning of the term “peer.” The results show that the respondents have different perceptions of the meaning of the term “peer” and that this difference affects the degree of agreement on the core elements of the concept. The study shows that it is important to investigate the concept of peer review in more detail and that the term “peer” should be clarified. The study also shows that CCA is a useful tool for investigating the extent to which a set of respondents shares a specific set of understandings.

The outer two circles represent the forecast impact and scientific validity, which are the goals that the forecasting and research communities aim to achieve. The middle circle represents the observational and modeling activities, which are the methods that researchers use to develop their forecasts and evaluate the accuracy of previous forecasts. In an ideal world, these three circles would be perfectly aligned, indicating that the forecasts scientists develop are based on the most up-to-date data and models and that forecast users receive the information they need to make informed decisions. However, the inner two circles can get out of alignment in several ways. First, observational and modeling activities may produce forecasts that are not useful to forecast users, perhaps because the forecast impact community has not effectively communicated their needs. Second, forecast providers may develop forecast products that are not based on the most up-to-date science, or the latest models may be unavailable to them. Finally, forecast users may not receive the information they need to make decisions, perhaps because they are not aware of the scientific uncertainty or because the forecast products are not consistent with the scientific findings. The arrows in the diagram indicate some of the factors that can cause misalignment between the different components of the forecast cycle. Forecast providers and forecast users must work together to understand these factors and ensure that the activities in the middle circle align with the impact and validity goals represented by the outer two circles.

samples.ref: Izinsizakalo zokubikezela zikazwelonke kanye namawebhusayithi ahlukahlukene ezentengiselwano ahlinzeka ngezibikezelo mayelana nokuthi isimo sezulu sizoba yini.
samples.hyp:
These predictions are based on mathematical models of the atmosphere that simulate its dynamics. Using the latest observations of temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, and so on, together with realistic initial conditions describing the present state of the atmosphere, these models can make skillful forecasts of the weather for one to two weeks into the future. Beyond that, though, their skill decreases rapidly, and forecasts made purely from the models are not much better than random guesses.

Now, a study published in Physical Review Letters by a team of researchers led by Shyam Hamal, at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, reports the results of an analysis of why current models are not able to make skillful forecasts beyond one to two weeks. The team used a novel approach to analyze the models’ performance in a realistic setting. In their analysis, the researchers found that the current models are fundamentally limited by the strong nonlinear effects present in the atmosphere. These effects are associated with the self-organization of convective storms, which are not well represented in the models. The researchers also note that the effects of convective storms on the large-scale flow are not well captured in the current generation of models. Thus, in order to make skillful forecasts of weather patterns on longer time scales, both of these problems need to be addressed in the development of future models.

– Michael Schirber

samples.ref: Kulolu cwaningo abacwaningi bakhethe ukubheka ukuthi abantu baseNingizimu Afrika naseNew Zealand bazisebenzisa kanjani izinsiza zokubikezela - omabili la mazwe anogu olude, kodwa anemiphakathi ehluke kakhulu nezimo ezisogwini.
samples.hyp:
In South Africa, where the study was conducted, there are many people living in poverty and without access to reliable weather information. In New Zealand, the government provides a lot of funding for research into weather and climate, and weather forecasts are considered very reliable.

The researchers used social media posts from 2008 to 2017 to find out how often people in each country used weather forecasts to plan their days and how reliable they considered the forecasts to be. They also looked at how the forecasts were used by the media and government agencies in each country.

The researchers found that people in South Africa used the forecasts more often than people in New Zealand. They used the forecasts to plan outdoor activities, but also to plan activities that depend on the weather for both countries, such as deciding whether to carry an umbrella. The people in South Africa considered the forecasts to be less reliable than those in New Zealand, and they were more likely to turn to other sources of weather information.

The researchers also found that the weather and climate information was not being used by the media and government agencies in either country to help the public. In New Zealand, weather information was used more often to plan activities that are weather-dependent, such as extreme sports, and to warn people about potential weather risks.

The researchers suggest that the results of this study could be used to help people in South Africa make better use of forecasting services. They also suggest that the results could be used to help improve forecasting services for both countries.

The researchers found that the more surfers were exposed to sharks, the less likely they were to have a fear of sharks. The surfers who had the most experience in the water were 70% less likely to have a fear of sharks than were novice surfers who rarely went in the water.

The study participants were all members of the Cape Town Surf Lifesaving Club. Photo: Surf lifesaving (iStockPhoto.com)


The researchers used a statistical analysis method known as a structural equation model (SEM). SEM is a sophisticated method of analyzing the relationships between multiple variables. It allows researchers to test theories by identifying which variables are related to one another and in what direction.

The study focused on the relationships between two groups of variables: demographic variables (sex, age) and shark-related variables (shark exposure, familiarity with sharks, experience with sharks, and fear of sharks). The researchers wanted to test the hypothesis that the relationship between sex and the fear of sharks in South African surfers is mediated (influenced) by the variable of experience with sharks.

"We found that New Zealanders are, in fact, pretty good at accurately forecasting weather conditions based on the information available to them," says Dr. James Renwick, Victoria University of Wellington climate scientist and lead author of the study. "But they don't do any better than chance when it comes to the more extreme events - the events that cause problems for them."

The researchers want to see tailored weather reports that warn of the risk of accidents or injury due to the weather. They hope the reports would include information about how the weather might make people unsafe, for example, wind speed and direction and how long it would last.

Dr. Renwick says the reports would not need to be too detailed. "People just want to know 'Is it safe to go sailing? Is it safe to go for a walk?'"

Co-author Dr. Anna Holloway says better weather reports are only part of the solution. People also need to become more aware of the uncertainty of weather forecasts. "We need to do a better job of communicating just how difficult it is to predict the start and end of such events."

Dr. Renwick says the public assumes weather forecasting is an exact science because they don't understand the limitations of the science and the difficulty of forecasting extreme weather events.

He says New Zealanders trust weather forecasts about as much as they trust the weatherman in a suit standing in front of a map on TV, which is not too surprising. "We as meteorologists have encouraged that image; it's a good simple image, but it does encourage that sense of exact prediction."

samples.src: A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions:
samples.ref: Indlela yokubamba iqhaza yokuhlola ukukhalipha kwesimo sezulu kokungenelela kwezolimo:
samples.hyp:
Case Studies From Sri Lanka and Zambia

Megha Acharya, Emily Barwick, Julia A. A. Mason, Mark T. Pearson, Lindsay A. Robertson, Daniel R. S. Kottelat, Arwin van Niekerk, Ivor L. Jones, and Graham J. Edwards

Climate change is one of the most significant threats to global food security. In response, new climate-smart agricultural interventions are being developed and deployed worldwide. However, there is no universal agreement on what constitutes a climate-smart intervention or the net environmental, social, and economic outcomes that they should deliver. Thus, there is a need to develop site-specific climate-smartness assessments to underpin the adaptive management and future decision making for agricultural interventions. This study aims to develop a participatory method to assess the climate-smartness of existing agricultural interventions. Two case studies were conducted in Sri Lanka and Zambia, using observations, interviews, and surveys to assess the climate-smartness of interventions against a set of climate-smart criteria. The study demonstrated the usefulness of the participatory approach in assessing the climate-smartness of interventions and disentangling the diverse and often contrasting outcomes that different stakeholder groups value. Further, it showed that interventions can be climate-smart through their design, implementation, and use, and that the climate-smartness of an intervention can be higher or lower depending on the context. This method will guide the design and implementation of new and existing climate-smart interventions, and help resolve trade-offs between different outcomes.

-Control Study was conducted in a rural area in northeast Tanzania where slavery was endemic in the early 20th century. The study population was approximately 10,000 residents drawn from 23 villages. The goal of the study was to find out if the descendants of former slaves are at a disadvantage in obtaining health services compared to descendants of people who did not experience slavery. The hypothesis was that former slaves and their descendants would be disadvantaged because of perceived and real social discrimination. The results of the study were that the descendants of slaves were indeed at a disadvantage in obtaining health services in the following areas: receipt of insecticide-treated bed nets, childhood vaccinations, and birth registration. They were also disadvantaged in the area of property ownership and inheritance. In the Lushoto study, slavery has been gone for almost 100 years, and yet the effects still remain. This is important because it shows that the effects of slavery continue to have an impact on society even after the practice has been eliminated.

This study aimed to identify and prioritise objectives for CSA in the context of South African grain farming. The objectives were identified through a literature study and interviews with agricultural experts. Subsequently, a questionnaire survey was conducted with South African grain farmers to prioritise the objectives. The results from the survey were analysed using the TOPSIS method. The findings from this study can be used to develop a decision support tool for grain farmers to evaluate and implement CSA practices on their farms. The study also provides insight into how CSA can be prioritised in the South African grain farming context. The study found that CSA objectives which were the most important for grain farmers and should therefore be prioritised are: 1) Maintaining or increasing yields, 2) Reducing production risks, 3) Reducing financial costs, 4) Managing water resources, 5) Managing soil fertility resources, 6) Managing soil physical resources, 7) Sequestering carbon, 8) Enhancing resilience and 9) Enhancing biodiversity. The objectives that were found to be the least important for grain farmers and should therefore be deb-prioritised are: 1) Managing weather risks, 2) Managing energy resources, 3) Managing greenhouse gas emissions and 4) Capturing and retaining nutrients.

samples.src: Here, we describe a new participatory protocol for assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions in smallholder practices.
samples.ref: Lapha, sichaza inqubo entsha yokubamba iqhaza yokuhlola ubuhlakani besimo sezulu sokungenelela kwezolimo emikhubeni yabalimi abancane.
samples.hyp:
The ‘climate-smart’ (CS) approach to agriculture emphasizes the need to increase productivity in a sustainable way while building resilience to climate change. However, there are currently limited methods for quantifying CS performance. We developed a six-step participatory protocol for assessing the CS potential of an agricultural intervention. The protocol was applied to three case studies in Kenya and Uganda. In each case study system, the protocol was implemented in two villages, and key informant interviews and quantitative surveys were conducted among a sample of farmers. The results showed that the protocol effectively captured differential CS performance across intervention sites. Additionally, the protocol generated locally relevant, quantitative targets for CS performance that can be used to track the impact of future interventions. The protocol is highly participatory and can be applied by practitioners with limited technical expertise. It provides a framework for agricultural practitioners, policy-makers, and investors to assess and compare the CS performance of different interventions, and to enhance the CS performance of interventions in the design and implementation phases. The protocol can also be used as a training tool to build capacity among local stakeholders to identify and quantify CS indicators in agricultural interventions.

samples.ref: Amasu amasha okuqapha asiza ososayensi kanye nabalimi ukulungiselela ukushintsha kwesimo sezulu.
samples.hyp:
A new technique for monitoring the abundance and distribution of soil invertebrates, called ‘pitfall trapping’, has been shown to be a useful tool for assessing the impact of climate change on soil biodiversity. This technique was used in a study of a warming trend in alpine tundra soil in the Swiss Alps, which was published recently in the open access journal Soil1.

Climate change is one of the most pressing global issues facing the world today. It is therefore important that scientists develop and use appropriate techniques for monitoring the impact of climate change across different ecosystems, and that farmers are given the tools they need to adapt to changes in their local climate.

Here, pitfall trapping was used to monitor changes in the abundance and distribution of soil invertebrates over time at 22 sites in alpine tundra soil in the Swiss Alps. The researchers compared the data with long-term data from nine of the sites, and with air temperature records from 14 alpine tundra sites, to carefully monitor the impact of climate change on soil biodiversity.

Soil invertebrates are generally classified into four groups: nematodes (roundworms), springtails, snails, and slugs. The results showed that there had been significant increases in the abundance of snails and slugs at all 22 sites between 2003 and 2012. The researchers also found that the distribution of springtails had shifted to higher elevations, in unison with increasing air temperatures.

The authors conclude that the pitfall trapping technique is a useful tool for monitoring the impact of climate change on soil biodiversity. They write in their paper, “Pitfall trapping is a powerful method for assessing the impact of climate change on soil fauna, and should be used more frequently in climate impact studies to assess changes in soil biodiversity and to improve our understanding of its drivers.”

It is hoped that these findings will be useful for scientists working to monitor the impact of climate change, and for farmers who need to adapt to changes in their local climate.

1. N. Eisenhauer, A. Risch, M. B. B. Römer, R. D. Bardgett. Increased grazing reduces the negative effect of warming on belowground food webs in alpine tundra. Soil, 2016; DOI: 10.1038/s41598.2016.30726

samples.hyp:
The researchers have developed a method that helps farmers and scientists work together to measure how well new practices, such as intercropping or using new seeds, protect crops against extreme weather conditions.

Climate change is causing more frequent and extreme weather conditions, such as heavy downpours and heatwaves, which threaten the food security of farmers around the world. To manage these risks, farmers and scientists are developing new farming practices. But current methods of measuring how well these work aren’t suitable for farmers to use, which means there is a risk they will not be taken up.

Publishing in the journal Nature Sustainability, a team from the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), the University of Reading and the University of Cambridge describe a new method they have developed to work with farmers to measure the impact of new farming practices. The method was tested in trials in Tanzania, working with sorghum and pigeonpea crops.

The team worked with 30 farmers to test the new method. Sorghum and pigeonpea were grown on neighbouring plots of land, with one plot being used to grow the current variety of each crop that farmers normally use, and the other plot being used to grow the same crop after a new farming practice was applied. For example, one plot of sorghum may have used organic fertilizer, while the other plot may have used inorganic fertilizer. The farmers were randomly allocated which plot would be used for each crop, meaning that each farmer would have one plot of land for each crop that was grown, using the current farming practice, and one plot of land for each crop that was grown using the new farming practice.

The team found that when the new practices reduced crop yields, the farmers were more likely to adopt and continue using them if they were given the choice. The farmers were more likely to choose to continue using the new practices if they protected their crops against the extreme weather conditions that are becoming more common due to climate change.

The method was able to show the specific circumstances in which new farming practices should be used. For example, the team found that pigeonpea, when grown in combination with sorghum, protected sorghum yields against heavy rainfall. The method also showed that this combination of crops should only be used in areas with high rainfall.

This research was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

The concept is a three-pronged approach that 1) increases productivity, 2) enhances resilience and 3) reduces or removes greenhouse gas emissions. 

A new study suggests that in the case of one such climate-smart agriculture practice — the practice of planting trees among coffee crops to protect them from the wind — the third part of the equation may not be true for every coffee-growing region. 

The practice of planting trees in coffee farms, known as “shade coffee,” is often lauded as a climate-friendly practice. 

The new study, published in Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, found that in Colombia, the practice actually led to an increase in methane emissions. 

“Shade coffee” is promoted as a “climate-smart” practice, but this study suggests that this may not always be the case. 

The finding doesn’t invalidate the practice, the study’s authors note, given its many other benefits to farmers and the environment. 

The study used a unique approach to measure emissions from the soil of 30 coffee farms in Colombia. 

The authors note that more research is needed to determine whether this finding is unique to this farming practice in Colombia, and whether other climate-smart agriculture practices have an impact on emissions. 

“Measuring methane emissions from tropical agricultural soils comes with various technical challenges,” says Dr. Julia Miller, lead author of the study and a scientist at the Joint Research Unit for Sustainable Agriculture (UMR1242 Alimentation et Nutrition au Fonctionnement de l’Homme), Université de Bordeaux, France. 

“By using a stable isotope approach, we were able to estimate methane emissions for the entire farm, rather than for a small area like other methods do.” This allowed the authors to collect data on 30 farms instead of the six farms that usual methods would allow. 

Dr. Samuel Myers

Dr. Samuel Myers

This extra data bolstered by the stable isotope approach revealed a regional pattern: methane emissions increased with the shade coffee farming. 

“While this was not what we hypothesized to find, the pattern we found makes sense when you consider that there are benefits and costs to this farming practice,” says Miller. 

The farms in the study were located in the Colombia region of Cauca, where coffee farms can be located at high elevations. This can make it very difficult to find a flat piece of land to plant, so farmers often have limited options for where to plant trees for the “shade coffee” practice.

Otherwise, yields could drop by 20% or more by 2050.

The new study, published in Nature Sustainability, used historical records to show that, in the face of climate change, crop variety is key to maintaining high yields. The researchers found that, in regions like Central America, South Asia, and the Near East, farmers have access to a wide range of crop varieties, and so are able to plant local seeds that are highly adapted to their region’s climate, ensuring high yields no matter what the temperature is. In these regions, farmers typically plant several different varieties of a given crop next to each other; research has shown that this increases yields, as it means that there are always some plants doing well, even if the temperature gets too high for others.

Unfortunately, this kind of diversity is lacking in many African countries. The new study compared global data on the yields and temperatures of more than 3,000 different crop varieties and found that African farmers are currently growing a very narrow range of crops, with little diversity. This means that they do not have access to the same crop varieties as farmers in other regions, many of which are better adapted to their specific climate. The study used this data to make models of what would happen to crop yields in different African countries if farmers adopted more diverse crop varieties. The models found that increasing diversity could maintain or improve yields in all of the regions analyzed.

For Tanzanian farmers, this would mean planting a potpourri of up to seven different varieties of a given crop, such as maize, sorghum, or rice. The study found that adopting this kind of “diversified farming” could maintain yields in the face of climate change. The study also found that a greater diversity of crops would also help to improve farmers’ livelihoods by increasing food security, allowing for more crops to be sold, and helping to maintain soil health.

The study was conducted in two phases. In the first phase, the researchers conducted a systematic review to identify and describe interventions that aim to improve food security and adaptability. The review was conducted in three steps. First, the researchers searched seven databases and 15 websites to identify relevant studies. Second, the researchers screened the studies and extracted the data. Finally, the researchers presented the findings in tables and graphs. In the second phase, the researchers conducted a realist evaluation of the included studies. The evaluation was conducted in two steps. First, the researchers identified key stakeholders and conducted 23 semi-structured interviews with them. Second, the researchers analysed the data and presented the findings in a report. The review identified 19 interventions, which were implemented in 13 low-income countries. Most of the interventions were implemented in Asia, followed by Africa and Latin America. The interventions targeted small-scale farmers, pastoralists, and fishers. The main outcomes of the interventions were increased food production and reduced food insecurity. The evaluation found that the interventions had a positive impact on the lives of the beneficiaries. The beneficiaries were able to grow more food, earn more income, and improve their nutrition. However, the impacts of the interventions were not long-lasting. The benefits of the interventions were lost when the external support ended, and the local capacity was not built. The study suggests that climate smart interventions can be effective in improving food security and adaptability in low-income countries. However, more research is needed to replicate the findings and identify the best practices.

samples.hyp:

Aim: To explore the concept of non-indigenous pathogens of vertebrate animals as invasive species, using South Africa as a case study. Methods: A literature survey to identify pathogens as invasive species, and an online survey of South African government departments and agencies to identify which non-indigenous pathogens are known to occur in South Africa. Results: A total of 114 non-indigenous pathogens of vertebrate animals, comprising 83 mammalian, 23 avian and 8 reptile species, were identified as invasive species. The online survey confirmed that 92% of these species had been recorded in South Africa, but information on their invasive status was not recorded for 50% of these species. Main conclusions: 1) There is a need to standardise the collection of data on non-indigenous species, including their pathogens, in order to facilitate a holistic view of biological invasions and to identify new invasive species early. 2) There is a need to develop and implement a predictive model for pathogen invasions that considers both the pathogen and its vector. 3) Some pathogen species may invade in association with their indigenous vectors, but then spread by vectors adapted to the invasive host. 4) Once a pathogen species has adapted to both its vector and the invasive host, it may become a target for classical biological control using its indigenous vector. 5) There is a need to improve international collaboration to control biological invasions, including those due to pathogens, e.g. by exchanging information on agent identification, taxonomy, and host range; and by sharing the costs of control.
Keywords: biological invasion, classical biological control, indigenous vector, invasive pathogen, non-indigenous pathogen.

Here, we review the literature on the introduction, spread and impacts of invasive alien species on disease dynamics in both historical and contemporary contexts. We show that the study of invasive alien species as disease organisms has the potential to shed light on the invasion dynamics of these species and the control of their populations. We discuss two broad mechanisms through which invasive alien species can affect the transmission of diseases: (1) the introduction of new diseases and disease vectors; and (2) the establishment of invasive species and their diseases in new regions, which can change the natural history and risk of emergence of existing diseases. We conclude with a discussion of the implications of our findings for future research and management of invasive alien species.

The introduction of the Zebra mussel into the Great Lakes of North America is a prime example of the potential for introduced pathogens to do great ecological and economic harm. The Zebra mussel is native to the Caspian and Black Seas, and was accidentally introduced into the Great Lakes via ballast water from ships. Zebra mussels have no natural predators in the Great Lakes, and they are filter feeders. As they filter their food, they also filter out other organisms (including pathogens) from the water column. The end result of this feeding behavior is waters that are, effectively, pathogen free. This has had two effects. First, it has allowed the growth and spread of new water-borne pathogens that were previously suppressed by the “normal” background microbial community in the Great Lakes. A second effect has been to potentially spread existing water-borne pathogens to new locations. This second effect has the potential to be devastating if the introduced pathogens have not been identified, and their virulence in their new location is not understood. This second effect is not unique to the Great Lakes. Any ecosystem that is invaded by a new organism that removes a large amount of microbial biomass from the system has the potential to experience the spread of existing pathogens.

samples.src: An evidence based surgical algorithm for management of Odontogenic keratocyst
samples.ref: I-algorithm yokuhlinzwa esekelwe ebufakazini bokuphathwa kwe-Odontogenic keratocyst
samples.hyp:
in pediatric age group: A prospective case series

Background: Odontogenic Keratocyst (OK) are cysts that arise from the rest of the oral and maxillofacial region. They have a unique biological behavior and a high recurrence rate, even after complete surgical cyst removal. There is no consensus on the best management approach for OK in the pediatric age group. The aim of this study was to propose an evidence based surgical algorithm for management of OK in the pediatric age group.
Methods: Prospective case series of OK in patients aged 10-20 years who were managed between January 2015 and December 2018 in a tertiary care maxillofacial institute. Data regarding the preoperative clinical examination, CT scan findings, operation notes, histopathology and follow up were recorded and descriptively analyzed.
Results: A total of 20 patients met the inclusion criteria. The mean age of the patient group was 14.2 years. All the patients showed recurrence of OK either on clinical examination or on CT scan within an average follow up period of 33.1 months (range 13.3-59.7 months). In this series, the recurrence rate was 100% and the mean time to recurrence was 25.6 months. 13 patients showed recurrence on CT scan alone, which was not appreciated on clinical examination. Based on these observations, an evidence based surgical algorithm is proposed for the management of OK in the pediatric age group.
Conclusions: A three staged algorithm is suggested for management of OK in the pediatric age group. The role of site of recurrence and size of cyst in influencing the recurrence rate is highlighted.

Therefore, surgical excision is considered the best treatment option. However, the aggressiveness of the odontogenic keratocyst is highly debated. A systematic search of international databases was performed for relevant articles reporting on the recurrence rates of the odontogenic keratocyst that were included in the meta-analysis. A total of 1,285 patients from ten published studies were included in the quantitative analysis. The pooled recurrence rate was 7.6% (95% CI: 5.8%, 10.7%) for all patients with odontogenic keratocyst. The type of surgical procedure performed and the presence or absence of intraoperative tumor invasion were identified as significant sources of heterogeneity (P<0.001). Further analysis revealed that the recurrence rate of the odontogenic keratocyst after enucleation was 24.4% (95% CI: 18.6%, 31.2%), after marginal mandibulectomy it was 9.1% (95% CI: 4.0%, 16.8%), and after conservative excision it was 3.1% (95% CI: 0%, 8.5%). The recurrence rate of the odontogenic keratocyst with intraoperative tumor invasion was 17.9% (95% CI: 13.2%, 23.5%), and that without intraoperative tumor invasion was 5.6% (95% CI: 3.3%, 8.7%). A conservative surgical protocol, marginal mandibulectomy, was shown to have the lowest recurrence rate. However, its use is limited by the extent of tumor invasion at the time of surgery. In patients without intraoperative tumor invasion, conservative treatment with excisional biopsy is a viable option. In patients with local tissue invasion, radical surgery with wide local excision should be considered. However, in those with evidence of vascular/lymphatic invasion, adjuvant therapy or follow up should be considered.

A team of researchers from the University of Malaya (UM) has suggested a few ways to improve the treatment of jaw disease.

The team’s study, published in the Journal of Oral Pathology and Medicine, showed that while the current treatment for jaw disease was effective, there was room for improvement.

Jaw disease, or idiopathic condylar resorption, is a rare condition where the lower jaw shrinks mysteriously. In some cases, it may grow abnormally.

This may cause other teeth to shift position, creating an uneven smile, and in severe cases, making it difficult to eat or speak.

The condition can occur in people of all ages, including children, but it often only affects women in their reproductive years, which scientists are keen to understand.

For the study, the team used X-ray images and 3D images of 23 patients with jaw disease and 16 individuals without the disease as a control group.

This suggests that surgical treatment solely focused on the jawbone may not be enough. Instead, researchers say a surgical procedure that targets both the soft tissue and the jawbone may be more effective.

The team also found that the condition causes changes in the lower jaw, upper jaw, and facial bone structure.

In the upper jaw, the maxillary sinus increased in size while the lower jaw had a higher rate of condylar resorption.

The maxillary sinus is an air-filled space in the bones of the skull.

The findings suggest that patients with idiopathic condylar resorption have normal facial structure, but the disease causes changes to their facial and jaw anatomy.

This means that doctors need to take a holistic approach to treating the disease by considering the changes in both the upper and lower jaw, in addition to the soft tissue.

samples.ref: Umgomo we-Synthetic SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV), i-MERS-CoV kanye ne-SARS-CoV: Ukuhlaziya okuqhathanisayo kwekhompyutha ukuphakamisa ama-epitopes omhlanganyeli
samples.hyp:
for vaccine design

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 has created a need for the development of vaccines and therapies. Due to the high sequence conservation of the spike (S) protein, which plays a key role in virus–cell attachment, it is a suitable target for the development of a vaccine. The aim of this study is to identify and characterize potential immunogenic epitopes of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV for the design of a synthetic peptide vaccine. Using the 5 most prevalent SARS-CoV-2 strains, the 5 most conserved epitopes were selected from the spike protein. For the epitopes identified in SARS-CoV-2, the sequence conservation and T-cell epitope prediction for HLA-A*:-, HLA-B*:-, HLA-DR*:-, and HLA-DQ*:-were analyzed. The most conserved epitope in the S protein was also identified in the S protein of SARSr-CoV and MERS-CoV. The results of this study suggest that this epitope has the potential to be a cross-reactive epitope that can be used in the design of a peptide vaccine that is capable of inducing a response in individuals previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 and also provides protection in individuals who have not been exposed to the virus. The epitope has a high binding affinity for several HLA class I alleles and the consensus sequence shows approximately 90% identity to the epitope from the S protein of SARS-CoV-2. Thus, this study proposes the development of a peptide vaccine consisting of a conserved epitope shared between the S proteins of SARS-like viruses, which has the potential to be a cross-reactive vaccine.

HCoV-229E is detected worldwide with a higher prevalence in children than in adults and is associated with common cold. The virus is transmitted by respiratory droplets and can cause upper and lower respiratory tract infections. The infection is usually self-limiting in healthy individuals and can be confused with other viral and bacterial respiratory tract infections. HCoV-229E has been detected in immunocompromised patients with pneumonia and in children with bronchitis, croup, and pneumonia. The virus has also been detected in cell cultures and in experimentally infected nonhuman primates. The virus enters cells via the ACE2 receptor. The binding of the receptor and the virus is mediated by the S protein, which is present as dimers in the virion envelope. The S protein is cleaved by the host cell protease furin and thus enables virus assembly and maturation in the Golgi apparatus. The S protein of HCoV-229E is approximately 1,300 amino acids long and shares 70% sequence identity with the S protein of SARS-CoV-2. The S protein of HCoV-229E, but not the S protein of SARS-CoV-2, can use the α subunit of the IL-6 receptor (CD126) for cell entry, which results in reduced virus replication and IL-6 production. The S protein of HCoV-229E can be cleaved by furin and by the cellular enzyme TMPRSS2, whereas the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 can only be cleaved by furin. The target binding site of coronavirus spike protein is highly conserved region, which is important for the development of vaccines and drugs. The aim of this study is to identify the conserved region of 2019-nCoV, SARSr-CoV and MERS-CoV, and compare the most common protein domain of three viruses, and predict the epitope of three viruses for the development of vaccines and drugs. The consensus motif design for the epitope of three viruses was predicted by the method of JCP. The epitope of 2019-nCoV, SARSr-CoV and MERS-CoV will provide a theoretical basis for the development of vaccines and drugs for the prevention and treatment of 2019-nCoV, SARSr-CoV and MERS-CoV infection.

A team of scientists from the US and the UK have compared the genome of the virus that causes Covid-19 to the genomes of other viruses in its family, to help understand how it may cause disease and to find treatments and vaccines.

The team, which includes researchers from the US National Institutes of Health and the University of Cambridge in the UK, used a technique called comparative genomic analysis to look at regions of the SARS-CoV-2 genome that are the same and different to regions of the genomes of bat coronaviruses, and human coronaviruses that cause the common cold.

They suggest that this information will help scientists develop treatments and vaccines to fight Covid-19.

The researchers also note that the analysis may help explain why some people infected with the SARS-CoV-2 virus develop severe disease, while others show no symptoms.

The team’s work is published in Science.

Coronaviruses have spikes on their surface, which the scientists think may be key to how the virus causes respiratory disease. To understand how SARS-CoV-2 may cause disease, the team compared the genetic instructions for making these spikes — called spike proteins — in the SARS-CoV-2 virus to those of other coronaviruses that cause respiratory disease in animals.

The scientists found that the spike proteins of SARS-CoV-2, and another animal coronavirus called SHC014, have a region that could be cleaved by a protease enzyme called furin. This cleavage is thought to activate the virus so that it can infect and destroy cells more easily.

Image: Comparative genome analysis suggests that the SARS-CoV-2 virus may have been activated by a furin enzyme before it infected people. Nature Portfolio/Science

The team compared the SARS-CoV-2 genome to those of 14 bat coronaviruses, and 7 coronaviruses that infect animals including ferrets, palm civets and pigs. They used this information to create a family tree for SARS-CoV-2, which helped them to understand when and where the virus may have originated.

The results suggest that the SARS-CoV-2 genome is most similar to the spike protein genome of a bat coronavirus called RaTG13. The virus was first isolated from a cave in the Yunnan province of China in 2013, but it is not known whether this was the animal from which the virus that caused the current pandemic was transmitted to people.

The SARS-CoV-2 virus has been circulating in the global population for well over a year now, and during this time it has evolved quite a bit. 

One of the main ways that the virus mutates is via the spike protein. This is the protein that the virus uses to bind to human cells, so any changes to this protein could potentially have major implications for the virus. 

A recent study1 looked at all of the available genome sequences from around the world, and this is what they found: There have been 71,213 non-synonymous mutations fixed in the SARS-CoV-2 genome since the start of the pandemic. This is a lot of mutations! And while a large proportion of these mutations either don’t change how the protein works, or actually reduce its function, there have been 30 mutations that have potentially increased function. 

The researchers then looked at which of these mutations were present in different countries / regions around the world. What they found was that there were four mutations that had arisen independently in different parts of the world; these are highlighted in red in the network diagram below. samples.ref: Ukushaya kwenhliziyo okungajwayelekile ezigulini ezinkhuvethe i-COVID-19: Ukubuyekezwa Okuhlelekile kanye nokuhlaziywa kwe-Meta
samples.hyp:
The study aimed to present the pooled estimates of prevalence and risk factors of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, and SCOPUS for studies to May 2021. Studies that reported the prevalence of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 were selected. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed using the Quality in Prognosis Study (QUIPS) tool. The main outcomes were prevalence of new-onset cardiac arrhythmias and risk factors of cardiac arrhythmias. The random-effects model was used and the prevalence was presented as the percentage and 95% confidence interval (CI).

A total of 2,751 patients with COVID-19 from 14 studies were included in this review. The prevalence of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 was 20% (95% CI 15%-25%). The prevalence of new-onset arrhythmias was higher in Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients (35%; 95% CI 25%-45%) than in non-ICU patients (14%; 95% CI 9%-19%). For patients who required mechanical ventilation, the prevalence was higher (39%; 95% CI 25%-53%) compared to those treated with high-flow nasal cannula (10%; 95% CI 3%-17%) or supplemental oxygen (14%; 95% CI 10%-17%). Patients with arrhythmias were more likely to require mechanical ventilation (OR 2.16, 95% CI 1.32-3.49; P<0.05), and had a higher mortality rate (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.49-3.48; P<0.05).

This review identified that the prevalence of new-onset arrhythmias in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 was 20% and arrhythmias were associated with higher mortality. Patients with arrhythmias were also more likely to require mechanical ventilation.

Keywords: COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2; cardiac arrhythmias; new-onset arrhythmias; systematic review; meta-analysis; prevalence; risk factors.

This study aimed to summarize the current understanding of the prevalence, mechanisms, and significance of new-onset cardiac arrhythmias in COVID-19 patients, and to explore the potential associations of cardiac arrhythmias with outcomes in COVID-19 patients.
Using the following search strategy, we identified articles on coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and cardiac arrhythmia. We then performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to summarize the pooled prevalence of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients and to identify the associations of cardiac arrhythmia with outcomes in COVID-19 patients.
A total of 2767 articles were identified initially. After stringent selection and assessment, 20 articles were included in the systematic review and 11 articles in the meta-analysis. The prevalence of cardiac arrhythmia in COVID-19 patients was estimated to be 19% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 14%-23%). In COVID-19 patients, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (SVT) were more prevalent than ventricular tachyarrhythmias (VT) or ventricular fibrillation (VF), with a pooled prevalence of 3% (95% CI: 2%-5%), 1% (95% CI: 1%-2%), and 0.3% (95% CI: 0%-0.6%), respectively. Patients with cardiac arrhythmia were more likely to have a poor prognosis than those without (pooled odds ratio [OR]: 2.42, 95% CI: 1.32-4.42, p = 0.003). However, no significant association was found between cardiac arrhythmia and 30-day (OR: 2.48, 95% CI: 0.77-7.98, p = 0.13) or 90-day (OR: 2.00, 95% CI: 0.88-4.54, p = 0.09) mortality.
Cardiac arrhythmia, predominantly supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, was not rare in COVID-19 patients. Patients with cardiac arrhythmia had a worse prognosis. More large sample-size studies with high-quality are needed to explore the associations of cardiac arrhythmias with outcomes and underlying mechanisms in COVID-19 patients, and to verify the findings in this meta-analysis.

Keywords: COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2; Cardiac arrhythmia; Prevalence

Patient’s verbal consent for participation in the study was considered as valid consent as it was explained to the patients that participation was voluntary and that refusal to participate would not affect the rights of the patients or their treatment in any way.

In this article, we will review some of the research that shows how Covid-19 can affect the heart and what the symptoms are.

Covid-19 and the Heart: What We Know So Far

Myocardial infarction, heart failure, and arrhythmia are some of the heart conditions that Covid-19 may cause. Here is what we know about how Covid-19 can affect the heart and what the symptoms are.

Myocardial Infarction and Heart Failure

Covid-19 can cause myocardial infarction and heart failure, and these conditions can be fatal. Myocardial infarction is a common heart condition that occurs when the blood supply to the heart muscle is blocked. This can cause damage to the heart muscle and even heart failure. Heart failure, on the other hand, is a condition in which the heart is unable to pump blood effectively. This can cause congestion in the lungs and other organs, leading to shortness of breath, fatigue, and swelling in the legs and feet.

Arrhythmia

Covid-19 can also cause arrhythmia, which is an abnormal heartbeat. Arrhythmia can be dangerous because it can lead to a lack of blood flow to the heart and other organs. This can cause chest pain, dizziness, and fainting.

Long Covid and the Heart

Some people who have recovered from Covid-19 experience symptoms of the disease long after their initial recovery. This condition is known as long Covid, and it can have a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, and shortness of breath. Long Covid can also affect the heart, and some studies have shown that it can cause inflammation of the heart muscle, also known as myocarditis, as well as damage to the heart’s blood vessels. This can lead to heart failure, arrhythmia, and other heart conditions.

In conclusion, Covid-19 can affect the heart in a number of ways, and these effects can be serious and even fatal. It is important to be aware of the potential risks and to seek medical attention if you experience any heart-related symptoms after recovering from Covid-19.

samples.hyp:
A Qualitative Analysis

Mariana Alvarado, BS, Joana Lavorato, PhD, and Martin M. Montoya, PhD

J Prim Care Ment Health. 2022 Jun 1:1-10. doi: 10.1177/21582440221101331. Epub 2022 Jun 1.

PMID: 35659552 | PMC: PMC9132527 | DOI: 10.1177/21582440221101331

Introduction: Primary care is a key entry point to the mental health care system. However, little is known about first-generation immigrants’ perceptions of mental health, specifically post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). This study aimed to fill this literature gap by qualitatively describing the viewpoints of first-generation immigrants regarding migration, mental health, and PTSD. Method: We conducted 12 individual semi-structured interviews with first-generation immigrants in Southern California. Participants were recruited through snowball sampling from community organizations. Data were analyzed using an inductive approach (open and axial coding) to identify dominant viewpoints in each category. Results: Three themes emerged regarding migration: (1) Pushed or pulled by external factors, (2) A long and difficult journey, and (3) A journey that changed us. Three themes emerged regarding mental health: (1) Mental health is a gift, (2) Mental health is a challenge, and (3) A need for a bicultural therapist. Three themes emerged regarding PTSD: (1) Traumatic experiences of migration, (2) Traumatic experiences prior to migration, and (3) The need to feel safe and feel heard. Discussion: Our findings suggest that it is not enough to provide access to mental health services to immigrants. Our results support the need for services to be culturally and linguistically relevant, as well as safe and nonjudgmental. Additionally, our results highlight the importance of training primary care providers to treat immigrant patients and to ask them about their perceptions of mental health and PTSD.

However, few studies have examined the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of migrants and refugees. This study examined the relative impact of pre- and post-migration stressors on the mental health of a sample of 337 migrants and refugees residing in the United States. The sample included 161 refugees and 176 documented and undocumented migrants who completed a survey measure that assessed several pre- and post-migration stressors as well as mental health. Results indicated that pre- and post-migration stressors were significantly and positively associated with each other. Multiple regression analyses indicated that post-migration stressors were a significant predictor of mental health after controlling for pre-migration stressors. Furthermore, interaction effects were found between study variables and migration status (i.e., refugee vs. migrant). For migrants, none of the main effects or interaction effects was significantly associated with mental health. For refugees, pre-migration stressors had a significant main effect on mental health above and beyond the effects of post-migration stressors. These findings suggest that for refugees, pre-migration stressors may have long-lasting effects on their mental health, and highlight the need for mental health interventions that address the unique stressors faced by refugees, particularly during the presettlement period. For migrants, on the other hand, it appears that post-migration stressors play a significant role in the mental health and PTSD of migrants above and beyond the effects of pre-migration stressors. This finding has important implications for practitioners who work with migrants and refugees, and highlights the need to assess mental health and PTSD symptoms holistically, by examining the contributions of pre- and post-migration stressors to mental health problems among migrants and refugees.

The situation in a refugee’s home country and the experience of leaving it can have a significant impact on refugees’ mental health, according to new research funded by the Nuffield Foundation and carried out by Dr Betul Duben of the University of Oxford and Dr Daize Haynes of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

The study, published today (Friday 30 April) in BMC Medicine, a BMC (BioMed Central) journal, used data from 2537 refugees aged 18 and over, who took part in the European Refugee Health Information System (ERHIS) study between 2014 and 2017.

ERHIS was a multi-centre study carried out in six European hospitals and one refugee health centre in Greece, which aimed to understand more about the health of refugees who had arrived in Europe by sea, and to develop a model of refugee health that could be used by refugee health services.

Refugees were asked about their experiences in their home country and during their migration, and completed standardised measures of mental health. The researchers also had access to medical records from the participating hospitals and health centres.

Dr Duben, who is based at the Department of Psychiatry at Oxford University, said: “To come to a new country as a refugee is obviously a stressful event, but our study shows that the experience in refugees’ home country prior to migration and during migration has a strong relationship with their mental health.

samples.src: Presence and Persistence of Amblyomma Hebraeum Augments the Burden of Heartwater in the Southern District of Botswana
samples.ref: Ubukhona Nokuphikelela kwe-Amblyomma Hebraeum Kwengeza Umthwalo Wesifo Senhliziyo Emanzi Esifundeni EsiseNingizimu ye-Botswana
samples.hyp:
Heartwater is a tick-borne disease of cattle, caused by the protozoan parasite, Ehrlichia ruminantium. The disease is transmitted by the brown ear-tick, Amblyomma hebraeum. The study area comprised the southern district of Botswana. The presence of A. hebraeum was investigated on cattle in the study area by attaching an excised tick to the base of the ear of 122 cattle in Maun, and 97 in Kasane. The number of ticks attaching to each cattle ear was recorded at 24 h intervals for 5 days. The experiment was repeated four times during the course of a year. The overall tick burden was high, with 67.95% of Maun and 100% of Kasane cattle infested. The mean number of ticks attaching to Maun cattle was 14.54, 16.63, 13.82, and 17.45 for the four trials, while for Kasane these values were 21.05, 13.17, 32.45, and 20.92, respectively. The high tick burdens recorded in this study would suggest that heartwater is a major constraint to cattle production in the southern district of Botswana. The severity of heartwater infection in cattle is determined by the number of parasites in the animal at any given time. The persistence of A. hebraeum on the host for periods exceeding 48 h is essential for the transmission of E. ruminantium. The results of this study indicate that A. hebraeum attaches readily to cattle and that the ticks persist on the host for periods longer than 48 h. These findings suggest that the presence and persistence of A. hebraeum in the study area augment the burden of heartwater. The high tick burden recorded in this study would also suggest that the control of A. hebraeum is essential for the control of heartwater in the southern district of Botswana.

The disease is caused by the rickettsia Haemoplasma (HW), which is transmitted to bovids by brown soft ticks, Amblyomma variegatum. The main objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of HW in cattle and to characterize the HW strains isolated from the infected animals. A total of 115 cattle from 11 farms in the Tuli Block area were screened for the presence of HW by using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The PCR amplification products were sequenced and the obtained sequences were compared to their respective gene sequences from public databases. The results showed that 11 out of the 115 cattle (9.57%) were infected with HW. All the positive animals were from farm groups A, C and D and the infection was found to be more prevalent in cattle >2 years of age. Sequence analysis of the 16S rRNA gene revealed that the HW strains from this study belong to the novel HW genotypes, HW1 (AF025408.1) and HW2 (AF025409.1), which have not been described or identified before. The two genotypes are distinct from each other and from the 14 known HW genotypes. The overall findings from this study indicate that HW is still a problem in the Tuli Block area of Botswana. However, the infection prevalence was low when compared to other studies conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, which reported prevalences ranging from 37.2 to 100%. This might be due to the implementation of a tick control programme by the Botswana Meat Commission (BMC), which has led to a reduction in the incidence of bovine diseases that are transmitted by brown soft ticks in Botswana. This is the first report of the detection and characterization of HW genotypes in Botswana. The characterization of HW genotypes will help in designing control and management strategies for HW in cattle.

The epidemiology of the disease is influenced by climate, with the majority of cases occurring in years following good rains when tick populations are at their highest. The study describes the seasonal pattern of heartwater in cattle in Botswana and the impact of the disease on national cattle population. The study used data collected from government veterinary services between the years 1988 and 1993. The data consisted of monthly heartwater mortality reports from all the districts of Botswana for the six years and the corresponding cattle population estimates for each district. The impact of heartwater on the size of the national cattle population was assessed by comparing the size of the cattle population estimated to have been present if there had been no heartwater mortality with the actual number of cattle reported to be present at the end of the six study years. The sub-districts were selected based on their ecological and climatic conditions. The collected ticks were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level and fed on sheep for 24 hours. DNA was extracted from tick guts and the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region of the ribosomal RNA gene was amplified using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The PCR products were sequenced and sequences were identified through BLAST search. A total of 204 ticks were collected. The most prevalent tick species was Amblyomma variegatum (96.08% of the collected ticks). The remaining 3.92% were Rhipicephalus evertsi (2.94%) and Rhipicephalus appendiculatus (0.98%). The ITS sequences of the collected tick species were identical to the sequences obtained from GenBank. The results of this study suggest that the ITS region of rRNA gene is useful for identifying tick species. The high prevalence of A. variegatum in the study area is a cause for concern because this tick is the vector for Theileria parva, the causative agent of East Coast Fever, the most economically important tick-borne disease of cattle in sub-Saharan Africa.

The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of A. hebraeum in the Southern District of Botswana. A total of 1,155 cattle from 13 villages were examined for the presence of A. hebraeum. The villages were located in the North-Eastern (5), Kweneng (5) and Southern (3) Districts of Botswana. The prevalence of A. hebraeum was determined by the detection of adult and nymph ticks. The seasonal pattern of A. hebraeum was also studied. The overall prevalence of A. hebraeum in cattle was 26.5% (304 of 1,155). The North-Eastern District had the highest prevalence of 38.0% followed by the Kweneng District (31.0%) and the lowest prevalence, 11.1%, was recorded in the Southern District. The prevalence of A. hebraeum was 24.4% in the wet season and 29.0% in the dry season. These results indicate that A. hebraeum is a serious constraint to livestock production in the Southern District of Botswana. Further research should focus on the development of management strategies for effective tick control in this district.
