This is according to a research done by Dr. Lucy Gibson from the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits) in Johannesburg, South Africa. The research was presented at the Geological Society of America (GSA) Supperannual meeting in Philadelphia, USA.
During the study, Dr. Gibson and her team focused on the Mbozama and Tugela river catchments in the Drakensberg mountains. The Drakensberg area is known for its diverse springs, which include the highest spring in the country, the Giant’s Castle Spring (the Olifants River rises there). The spring has a flow of 15 million litres of water a day.
The team collected surface and spring water samples and analysed them. The aim was to look at the water chemistry of the Drakensberg springs and to determine if the springs are recharged from surface waters or from groundwater.
The results of the research showed that the soil and bedrock in the Drakensberg are highly weathered. This means that they are eroded and have changed their original composition, due to the climate change that occurred a long time ago. The soil is mostly made out of sand and the bedrock is made out of granite and metamorphic rock.
The high weathering of the rocks affects the water chemistry of the springs. The water that flows through the soil and bedrock gets chemically changed by the weathered rock. This means that the quality of the water that comes out from the ground as a spring is of a higher quality than the water that goes into the ground.
Dr. Gibson said that the Drakensberg mountains are a significant water tower in South Africa. Most of the water that is produced in the Drakensberg mountains supplies major cities like Durban, Johannesburg and Cape Town with drinking water.
The team’s next step is to look at the water that goes into the ground to see how it is changed in the soil and bedrock before it comes out as a spring.

A study by the University of Ibadan has revealed that the current vaccines used in Nigeria against heartwater, a tick-borne disease that affects animals, are not effective on the indigenous goat and cattle breeds in the country.

The disease, which is caused by the protozoan parasite, trypanosoma congolense, is transmitted by the brown ear tick, or solenopotes capensis.

Point of care testing (POCT) is a fast developing field in diagnostic medicine. Tests are performed in close proximity to the patient and do not require the tests to be run in a centralized laboratory. There are several advantages of POCT, such as improved clinical outcomes, reduced healthcare costs, and the ability to provide better care to patients in remote locations. However, there are also several technical and logistical challenges to implementing POCT. These challenges are different in different parts of the world, and in this article we focus on two countries, India and South Africa, which are facing several common barriers to the implementation of POCT. After introducing POCT and the challenges associated with implementation, we focus on the current situation in India and South Africa, and suggest possible solutions to overcome the barriers to POCT in these countries.

Point of Care Testing

Point of care testing (POCT) involves performing a test close to the site of patient care, and the results of the test are available within minutes. Such tests can be performed by non-specialized personnel, which eliminates the need to send samples to a centralized laboratory for testing. POCT is also known as point-of-care diagnostics, near patient testing, bedside testing, or sentry testing. POCT can be performed using portable equipment, which is often based on technologies such as biosensors or microfluidics. POCT is a fast developing field and several major diagnostic companies are offering tests based on POCT technologies.

There are several advantages of POCT. One of the most important ones is that the test results are available within minutes. For many diseases, especially infectious diseases, the test results can dictate the further course of action. For example, a positive test result for HIV may require the patient to start antiretroviral therapy immediately, which can be done only if the test results are available promptly. Another advantage of POCT is that it allows medical personnel to perform tests outside central laboratories, which saves time and reduces the pressure on central laboratories. POCT also allows patients to receive their test results and start treatment immediately. This is especially useful for patients who need continuous monitoring of certain health parameters, such as glucose levels in diabetic patients. POCT can also improve the quality of care in remote locations, where it is often difficult to transport patient samples to central laboratories. Finally, POCT can reduce healthcare costs by reducing the need for laboratory staff, building dedicated laboratory space, and purchasing expensive laboratory equipment.

Published on: 1 December 2020

By Alex Wilks, Senior Editor

The COVID-19 pandemic has shone a light on the world’s healthcare systems and the fragility of many of them.

In addition to highlighting deep-seated issues with the US’s system, the pandemic has also shown that poor testing regimes can have a profound impact on patient care. This has been evident in the US, where a lack of testing has left many in limbo not knowing whether they are positive or negative for SARS-CoV-2, and in India and South Africa, where testing issues have been a major factor in a slow and underwhelming COVID-19 testing and healthcare response.

Testing is an integral part of any healthcare system. It allows doctors and nurses to get information about a patient’s health, allowing them to make an accurate diagnosis and the best treatment plan. This is as true for COVID-19 as it is for more established conditions such as HIV, TB, malaria and more. Point-of-care testing (POCT), which allows testing to take place in a non-specialized laboratory setting, is particularly important in resource-poor countries where specialized labs may be few and far between. POCT can help to make sure that a patient’s test is conducted as close to their home or local healthcare center as possible, allowing them to access their results and commence treatment as soon as possible.

However, a recent paper published in Science Direct, titled ‘Poor point-of-care testing in South Africa and India: the devil is in the details’, has highlighted the fact that POCT in these two countries is not living up to its promise. The paper, written by Yoleka M. Ngcobo, T. Jacob John, and Shobna D. Sturrock, argues that in both India and South Africa, a lack of standardization, poor training of staff, and issues with the development and translation of tests into local languages have hampered the effectiveness of POCT.

The authors cite multiple examples of issues with POCT in South Africa and India. This includes tests that do not follow WHO guidelines, a lack of post-test training for staff, and issues with the translation of tests into local languages such as Afrikaans and Hindi, among others.

The authors also highlight the fact that in both countries, POCT is often conducted in a central laboratory, rather than at a point-of-care, meaning that the very thing that POCT is designed to help—quicker, more convenient testing— is not taking place.

The term point-of-care is also used to refer to the actual device or instrument used to perform the test. POC testing is also known as near-patient testing or bedside testing.

The term point-of-care is often used interchangeably with the term point-of-care testing (PCT), but PCT refers specifically to the testing itself, while point-of-care refers to both the device and the testing itself. The term POCT is sometimes used to refer to the entire process, including the preparation of samples for testing.

The use of POC tests is also known as “integrated care”, which is a model of healthcare that aims to provide the right care, at the right time, and in the right place, by the right person, with the best possible outcome for the patient. This model of care is designed to be patient-centered, with the goal of improving the quality of care and reducing healthcare costs.

POC tests are typically quick and easy to use, and they can provide results in minutes, rather than hours or days. This can be especially important in emergency situations, where rapid results can help healthcare providers make life-saving decisions more quickly.

There are many different types of POC tests available, for a wide range of medical conditions. Some common examples include:

- Blood glucose tests for diabetes management
- Pregnancy tests to determine if a woman is pregnant
- Cholesterol tests to assess heart disease risk
- Strep throat tests to diagnose strep throat infections
- HIV tests to screen for HIV infection

POC tests are becoming increasingly common in healthcare settings, as they offer many advantages over traditional laboratory testing. POC tests are typically less expensive, quicker, and easier to use than laboratory tests, and they can provide results in a more convenient location for the patient. Additionally, POC tests can be performed by healthcare providers with minimal training, which can help to improve access to healthcare, especially in remote or underserved areas.

A conceptual analysis was conducted of 44 relevant articles, which included empirical studies of critical care from 1971 to 2018, as well as articles that provided explicit definitions of critical illness or critical care. Data were coded by hand using a constant comparative method. Eight themes were identified: (1) critical illness as an extreme form of disease; (2) critical illness as a disease-related threat to life; (3) critical illness as a disease-related inability to function; (4) critical care as a treatment; (5) critical care as an intensive treatment; (6) critical care as an intensive treatment requiring advanced practice; (7) critical care as an intervention for the interprofessional team; and (8) critical care as a time-limited intervention. Based on the study findings, three explicit definitions of critical care are proposed: (1) critical care is the use of advanced practice interventions in the resolution of time-limited, life-threatening, disease-related health issues; (2) critical care is an interprofessional team approach to the treatment of a patient with a life-threatening, time-limited health issue, requiring advanced practice; and (3) critical care is an intensive, advanced practice intervention in the resolution of a life-threatening, disease-related health issue. This study offers potential consensus definitions for critical illness and critical care, and contributes to a shared understanding of the concepts.

A secondary aim was to assess the feasibility of conducting the survey, and to explore the differences in concept use across clinical specialties.

The results of the scoping review are presented as a list of concepts and their most common uses in clinical practice and research, as identified by experts. The results of the survey are presented as concept rankings, word definitions, and an assessment of ease of completion of the survey, by specialty. We found good agreement between concept rankings from the survey, with a global top three ranking of 1) pain and its severity, 2) functional status and quality of life, and 3) comorbidity. We propose to define critical illness rather than disease because the definition of critical illness underpins our understanding of the continuum of illness and guides the development of health services and the allocation of resources. In this review, we describe the historical development of the concept of critical illness, its measurement and classification, the proposed definition of critical illness, and the implications of the definition for future research and health services. We performed a literature review for this work. We define a hierarchy of health states that includes well, sick, and critically ill. We explain why the proposed definition of critical illness provides a useful framework for the classification of health states. We describe the implications of the definition for future research and health services, including health services research on the outcomes of individuals at each end of the continuum of illness, research into the causes and effects of conditions that are at risk of deterioration to critical illness, and the development of early warning systems for individuals at risk of deterioration to critical illness. We propose a research agenda that includes the evaluation of the utility of the definition of critical illness for classifying health states and for guiding the allocation of resources.

English:
This concept analysis is the first study to systematically describe the uses and definitions of the concepts critical illness and critical care. Critical illness is a potentially lethal disease process associated with multiple organ dysfunctions and/or acute life-threatening abnormalities in the function of more than one body system. Critical care is specialized organ system support for acutely ill patients. The purpose of this paper is to describe the history, empirical observations, and uses of the concepts critical illness and critical care. A literature search was conducted for the past 10 years using MEDLINE, CINAHL, and Ebscohost. The concept of critical illness was unclear and lacked consistency in definitions. There were more research studies on the concept of critical care. Most of the studies on critical care were written by nurses in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting. Nurses are the primary health care providers who are responsible for the management and care of the critically ill patients. The concept of critical care was found to have a meaning that was consistent with its definitions. There was controversy about whether the outcome of death should be an essential component of the definition of critical illness. The most recent 2016 American College of Critical Care Society definition of critical illness included the outcome of death. The historical development of the ICU was described. The concept of critical illness will be useful for nursing researchers to examine how nurses provide care for the critically ill. The concept of critical care provides direction for nurses to provide evidence-based care for their patients in the ICU.

The re-definition of “critically ill” patients and their care has been published in the Journal of Critical Care.

First author Dr. Marcello Maggiolini, from the Department of Anesthesia and Critical Care at the Humanitas Research Hospital, said: “Our study provides a new definition of critically ill patients and their care, which can be used to improve the quality of care delivered to this patient population. We believe that our findings will help to improve the quality of care delivered to this patient population, and ultimately improve patient outcomes.”

The study, which used data from the SAFER (Safe Health Care for Patients’ End-of-Life Decision Making) project, found that the current definition of critically ill patients, as determined by the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II, is limited in its ability to identify patients who are at the end of life. The APACHE II is an evaluation system widely used in intensive care units (ICUs) to classify a patient’s severity of illness and to determine which patients are critically ill.

The study found that the APACHE II identified 48% of patients as critically ill. However, by using a new definition of critical illness, which included variables such as increased risk of death, increased use of life-sustaining treatments, and decreased quality of life, the researchers were able to identify 100% of patients who were at the end of life.

The study also found that critically ill patients who were at the end of life were more likely to receive intensive care and life-sustaining treatments, such as mechanical ventilation and hemodialysis. However, these patients were also more likely to receive treatments that were not consistent with their preferences and values. The researchers found that by using a new definition of critical illness, which took into account a patient’s preferences and values, it was possible to identify treatments that were not consistent with a patient’s preferences and values and to avoid them.

Senior author Dr. Samuele Remuzzi, from the Department of Nephrology and Dialysis at the Humanitas Research Hospital, said: “Our study shows that by re-defining the meaning of “critically ill” patients and their care, it is possible to improve the quality of care delivered to this patient population. They said the definitions can be used by health care workers, community leaders and others to describe the severity of the condition in individual patients, to determine whether specific treatments are working, to predict the likelihood of death, and to design and test new interventions.

Dr. Robert Heyderman, from Malawi's College of Medicine in Blantyre, said: "We've long known that HIV causes immune deficiency, but we've only recently begun to understand the complexities of the disease. It's these new insights that allow us to identify those patients who are most at risk. It also enables health workers to have a simple tool that they can use in the clinic to help them to identify the people whose condition is most severe.

Professor Janet Weber, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said: "These new clinical definitions, together with measures of CD4 cell count and plasma viral load, will allow better standardisation of the way HIV infection is classified for research purposes.

She added: "This will allow us to better understand how HIV disease affects different groups of patients, which will have implications for future prevention, treatment, and cure strategies."

The researchers say their definitions could also be applied in other diseases where more than one clinical stage is recognized.

They say a person's stage of disease progression is important both from the perspective of the individual and also in terms of the broader epidemic. As an individual's disease progresses they are at increased risk of developing other health problems, increased morbidity, and of dying from HIV or other opportunistic infections. From a broader public health perspective, advanced stages of disease are associated with increased transmission of HIV.

Dr. Sarah Loynd, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said: "By classifying patients according to their disease stage, we can ensure that the right people are targeted in trials of treatments and behavioral interventions, which are an important part of the global response to HIV."

Professor Chris Dye, from the World Health Organization, said: "These new staging definitions for HIV infection will help us to compare data across different research studies and to monitor trends in the epidemiology and burden of disease.

Abstract
Plasmodium parasites are responsible for several devastating human diseases, including malaria. During the early stages of Plasmodium liver infection, the human host responds to the pathogen with an inflammatory immune response that reprograms liver organ homeostasis, leading to hepatic pathology and extracellular parasite growth. To investigate the role of the host in regulating parasite microtubule dynamics during infection, we used a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screening approach to identify host factors that when disrupted result in dysregulated microtubule organization. We identified 16 genes on 15 chromosomes that when disrupted by CRISPR-Cas9 resulted in increased parasite motility in the early stages of infection. One of the genes, CENPJ, was further investigated, and we demonstrated that CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of CENPJ in hepatoma cells or in human primary hepatocytes enhanced parasite motility and infection. We also demonstrated that CENPJ localizes to the centrosome in hepatoma cells and that during Plasmodium infection CENPJ localizes to both the centrosome and the parasite–host interface, suggesting a role for CENPJ in modulating microtubule dynamics at the cell periphery. We also demonstrated that P. berghei parasites expressing a centrosomal GFP tag displayed altered microtubule organization and increased motility when expressed in CENPJ-knockout Huh7 cells. Together, these data suggest that CENPJ functions as a regulator of microtubule dynamics during the early stages of Plasmodium liver infection.

The scientists used a combination of cutting-edge imaging techniques and genetic manipulation to peer inside the cells of malaria parasites, and observe the ins and outs of their replication process.

They found that two organelles, the mitochondrion and the apicoplast, are hijacked by the parasites to help them make the necessary proteins to reproduce.

Malaria is a growing problem in parts of the world, with nearly half of the world's population at risk of infection. In 2016, there were an estimated 216 million cases of the disease, resulting in 445 000 deaths, most of them children. The disease is caused by a parasite that is transmitted to people by the bite of an infected mosquito. samples.src: Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort
samples.ref: Ukuhlasela Kwezinto Eziphilayo Njengengxenye Yomzamo Wokucwaninga Ngezinguquko Zomhlaba waseNingizimu Afrika
samples.hyp:
South Africa, like many other countries, is experiencing rapid environmental change as a consequence of global change. One of the most pressing issues confronting South Africa is that global change is likely to exacerbate biological invasions. South Africa has a long history of biological invasions and has hotspots of invasive plant species with, for example, a higher number of alien plant species at protected areas than would be expected by chance. In addition, biological invasions in South Africa are likely to threaten the survival of many species of conservation concern. For example, the number of invasive animal species listed as predators, competitors, or herbivores in South Africa is 21%, 38%, and 12%, respectively, of the total number of animal species introduced into the country, and invasive plant species are listed as threats in 45% of the threatened animal species assessments in South Africa. There are also a number of examples where biological invasions are likely to impact the provision of ecosystem services. For example, invasive species are identified as major threats to the provision of water through modification of water tables and stream flow, and the regulation of water quality and erosion. This article argues that biological invasions should be considered as an important component of global change research in South Africa and should be given greater consideration in South Africa’s global change research program. In order to make this case, three issues are discussed. First, the extent of biological invasions in South Africa is reviewed. Second, the potential impacts of biological invasions and the interactions with other global change processes are assessed. Third, the current research capacity to study biological invasions in South Africa is evaluated. On the basis of this evaluation, arguments are made for increasing the focus on biological invasions in South Africa’s global change research program.

Keywords: Biological invasions, Exotic species, Global change, Invasive species, South Africa

We identified 688 publications, from which we extracted 1090 data records. Using a series of indicators, we estimated the cumulative ecological impact of these drivers on South African ecosystems. About half of the publications focused on biological invasions, with a further 20% and 15% on climate change and overharvesting, respectively. The total impact of these drivers was high, with 72% of ecosystems in South Africa experiencing a negative impact from one or more of these drivers. The estimated cumulative impact of biological invasions, climate change, overharvesting, habitat change, pollution, and atmospheric CO2 on South African ecosystems is 55%, 32%, 32%, 26%, 25%, and 22%, respectively. A spatial analysis of the impact of these drivers shows that most of the impact is on the Western Cape, followed by KwaZulu-Natal, with the least in the Northern Cape. Our results highlight the need to pay greater attention to the combined impact of multiple stressors on biological diversity and ecosystem processes.

The Global Burden of Disease, Risk Factors, and Impact on Population Health Study (GBD 2016) is the most comprehensive global analysis of risk factors for death and disability, as well as their trends over time and differences across countries. The GBD Study provides a systematic synthesis of population-level data on 21 risk factors for 33 diseases and injuries and 84 potential risk factors. These data are used to generate estimates of the disease burden attributable to each of these risk factors. The GBD 2016 study identified 15 groups of risk factors, including 11 behavioral, 3 environmental, and 1 group of metabolic risks. The 11 behavioral risk factors are related to diet, physical inactivity, alcohol and drug use, tobacco use, and sexual behavior. The 3 environmental risk factors are air pollution, secondhand smoke, and unsafe water and poor sanitation. The metabolic risk is high body mass index (BMI) and a short height. The GBD 2016 study also assessed the contribution of 84 potential risk factors to death and disability. Research has shown that human induced environmental change is occurring at an unprecedented rate and has wide reaching effects on ecosystems (Scheffer et al. 2015). In a recent publication, a team of researchers led by Dr. Louis du Preez of the DWT-NNS Centre of Excellence for Invasion Biology (Cebio) at Stellenbosch University, and including Cebio Director, Professor Bruce Wilgen, compared the number of South African scientific publications on invasive species and habitat change, with those for other global biodiversity change drivers such as climate change, over the past 30 years. They found that the research output for invasive species was roughly similar to that for climate change, and significantly higher than that for habitat change. These results are in line with the outputs of two previous studies – one regional and one global – that the team also conducted and that matched their current findings.
In the study, published in the journal Diversity and Distributions, the researchers acknowledge that invasive species may not pose the same threat to biodiversity globally as they do in the tropics, where species diversity is highest. However, the team believes that their results highlight the need for South Africa to maintain or increase its efforts and investments in research on invasive species, to inform management decisions and mitigate threats to biodiversity in South Africa.
The team also recently conducted a global review of how changes in the abundance of native species, due to invasive species, affect biodiversity. The study, published in the journal Biological Invasions, found that, although the effect of increased abundance of native species on biodiversity varies according to the invaded community, native species’ abundance typically decreases with increasing levels of biological invasions. The researchers therefore call for more research on the effect of changes in the abundance of native species on different community types, and on the effects of native species reintroduction as a management strategy to mitigate the negative effects of biological invasions.
These two studies form part of the team’s research for the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Global Species Assessment, which is due to be updated in 2026. The team’s most recent publication provides an overview of global research on biological invasions over the past 30 years, which will help to inform the next assessment. The team’s global and regional findings for the IUCN assessment are also an important input for the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) Global Assessment of Land Biodiversity, which is currently being finalised.

We reviewed the number of invasive species, the number of studies, and the year of publication of studies on invasive species in South Africa. We used a literature review to identify the year when a study could be considered as the first to report on a species as invasive. We used a species distribution model to predict the year of arrival of all known invasive species in South Africa. We found 166 invasive species and 186 studies. The number of species and studies increased over time, but the increase was not linear. The first study reporting species as invasive was published 13–31 years after the first record of arrival of that species. The predicted year of arrival of all invasive species was between 1925 and 2004. The number of studies did not correlate with the number of invasive alien tree species nor with the number of years since the first alien tree invasion. The number of studies increased for all taxonomic groups except for protists, but the increase was not linear and did not correlate with the number of species in the group. The year of first reporting of a species as invasive did not correlate with the number of studies on that species. The year of first reporting of a species as invasive was related to the number of studies for taxa with > 50 studies, but not for taxa with less than 50 studies. The number of studies for insect species increased exponentially. The year of first reporting a species as invasive could provide a basis for exploring complex interactions among biological, social, and economic factors that influence management of invasive species.

Abstract

Invasive alien species, climate change and human activities are among the greatest threats to the survival of biodiversity in South Africa. However, the combined effect of these stressors on biodiversity remains poorly understood. Here, we argue that change in the distribution and abundance of invasive alien species is likely to be affected by both climate change and various human activities, and that the combined effect of these drivers on invasive alien species is likely to be greater than the sum of their individual effects. As such, researchers in South Africa need to consider the combined effect of multiple stressors, including invasive alien species, climate change and various human activities on biodiversity, and adopt an integrated research approach to better understand these stressors and their interaction. Without this combined effect research, management strategies will likely fail to achieve their goals of safeguarding biodiversity in South Africa.

The aim of this study was to examine the research on substance use among South African adolescents and to identify gaps in the literature that can be addressed in future research. Two databases were searched from their inception to February 2018. Studies were selected if they (a) focused on substance use among adolescents aged 12–19 years; (b) reported prevalence of substance use; (c) were published in peer-reviewed journals; and (d) were conducted in South Africa. The literature search yielded 41 articles. Results showed that there was a general increase in the prevalence of substance use among adolescents between 2000 and 2013. Prevalence of use of alcohol, tobacco, marijuana, cocaine, heroin, ecstasy, LSD, and prescription and nonprescription medications was estimated at 7%, 7%, 6%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 1%, and 5%, respectively. A number of research gaps were identified: (a) little is known about substance use among sexual and gender minorities; (b) there is a lack of research on the use of prescription and nonprescription medications; (c) research on the use of hallucinogens is limited; and (d) research on the use of volatile substances, tobacco, and alcohol among adolescents living with disabilities is also limited.

This is the first time a comprehensive look has been taken at this subject, and it is hoped the new database will help improve the understanding of vehicle interactions and ultimately improve road safety.

Dr Simon Moore, from the University of Birmingham’s Centre for Accident Investigation, said: “There has been a lot of interest in the idea of automated vehicles to improve road safety, but it will be many years until they are on our roads in any numbers.

“Even if they are a success, there will still be a need for humans to drive in a shared network with automated vehicles.

“Very little is known about how vehicles interact with each other when driving. This project has brought together a team of researchers to look at the available evidence and it shows that although there are many types of interaction, most are positive.

“However, the evidence is largely based on small numbers of vehicles and so we don’t know what happens when large numbers of vehicles are involved, or how the findings can be transferred to real world driving.

“Driverless vehicles will need to be able to make decisions based on the decisions that other vehicles are making and so this work forms an important basis for the future of road safety.”

The project was a collaboration between the University of Central Lancashire, the University of Northampton, the University of York, TRL and the University of Birmingham.

Professor Martin Potter from UCLan said: “We must be careful in making assumptions about how people drive and what that means for the design of the roads and vehicles of the future.

“Although there are many types of interaction between vehicles, the project has found that the majority are positive, with vehicles slowing down to let other vehicles in or avoiding a collision.

“The project has revealed a lack of empirical evidence and there is a need for more research in this area to take place before we begin to rely too heavily on automated vehicles.”

The study was a collaborative effort involving 14 authors from various institutions across the country. The project was led by Professor David Richardson of the Department of Conservation Biology and Ecological Sciences at the University of Cape Town.

Professor Richardson says ecosystems across the world are affected by changes in climate, land use, invasive species, pollution and poaching. "Understanding how multiple drivers interact with each other, and how this affects biodiversity and ecosystem functions is a major goal of global change research. This knowledge is essential for developing policies and making management decisions that can mitigate the negative impacts of these changes on people as well as on the natural environment."

The research team used data on 118 species of plants, birds, mammals and reptiles recorded from 216 protected areas in South Africa. For each of the drivers of global change, the team examined how much area of each protected area has changed. "We then used computer models to simulate how the combined effect of these changes in each protected area affects the 118 species," says Professor Richardson.

The results showed that the different drivers of global change had contrasting effects on biodiversity. "Some drivers cause biodiversity to decline while others cause it to increase. Our results also show that the combined effect of these drivers on biodiversity is not simply the sum of their separate effects," he says.

Professor Richardson says it is important to take into account the opposing effects of some of the drivers, and to recognise that one driver may have conflicting effects on different components of biodiversity. "For example, increased atmospheric carbon dioxide may benefit plants by making more water available for them to use, but it has the opposite effect on animals by reducing the quantity of water in rivers and wetlands."

Professor Richardson says the research highlights the need for policies and management interventions to maintain the health of South African ecosystems. "Our results suggest that a composite effect of all the drivers of global change we examined combined to reduce the area of protected areas. If true, this has major implications for biodiversity conservation as protected areas are known to contain a large proportion of the country's biodiversity."

The study, published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, is an example of how South Africa's national research priorities are being advanced by the National Research Foundation (NRF) through its South African Environmental Observation Network (Saeon) project. The NRF established the Saeon project to develop long-term, ecological research in South Africa and to create a national network of monitoring sites in partnership with universities, ecological organisations and other stakeholders

The dynamics of SOM are a function of the input and storage of organic matter and the outputs by decomposition. Forest management can alter SOM through changes in the input, storage, and output of organic matter. The changes in input are caused by changes in species composition and composition-dependent dynamics, harvest intensity and frequency, and site preparation intensity. The changes in output are caused by changes in species composition, harvest intensity and frequency, site preparation intensity, and decomposition- and species-dependent dynamics. The changes in storage are caused by changes in species composition and composition-dependent dynamics, harvest intensity and frequency, site preparation intensity, and decomposition- and species-dependent dynamics. The potential of forest management to alter the input, storage, or output of organic matter is a function of the differences between the reference management and the alternative management. The reference management is a point of comparison for management treatments. The alternative management is the management being evaluated for its effects on SOM. The direction and magnitude of the potential effects of forest management on the input, storage, and output of organic matter are a function of the differences between the reference management and the alternative management and the response function of SOM to the management treatment. Forest management can have positive, negative, or no effect on the input, storage, or output of organic matter.

Here, we examine the influence of resource availability and grazing pressure on the site occupancy of a savannah mammal, the yellow-spotted hedgehog (Atelerix frontalis) using a presence-absence approach. We conducted 68 radiocollar captures of A. frontalis in a miombo woodland in South Africa during 2013/2014. Individual hedgehogs were tracked for 3–7 days and the influence of environmental variables on site occupancy determined using occupancy modelling. The best model included minimum temperature, relative humidity, soil moisture, canopy cover and grazing pressure as environmental predictors of site occupancy. At low relative humidity and soil moisture levels, and during periods of high minimum temperatures, site occupancy was significantly higher. Occupancy was also higher on sites with high canopy cover and low grazing pressure. Our results suggest that woodlands with high canopy cover, high humidity and moisture levels and low grazing pressure are important for maintaining SOM and C variability in miombo woodlands. These results are important for understanding the role of miombo woodlands in carbon sequestration and climate change and for incorporating this variability into future monitoring and management strategies for carbon storage in these woodlands.

These factors were pH, clay content, sand content, fine silt content, coarse silt content, colour (Blexedil), organic C, exchangeable Ca, and exchangeable Mg. Multiple linear regression analysis showed that SOM could be predicted from clay content, exchangeable Ca, exchangeable Mg, fine silt content, and sand content. The relative importance of these edaphic factors to SOM was calculated and clay content was the most important, with 32.4% of the variation in SOM explained by this factor. This was followed by exchangeable Ca with 15.4%, exchangeable Mg with 13.3%, fine silt content with 11.3%, and sand content with 10.3%. The results showed that SOM was significantly and positively correlated with exchangeable Ca, exchangeable Mg, and fine silt content, and negatively correlated with sand content. The results of this study suggest that the most important edaphic factors influencing SOM in miombo woodland of Luanshya are clay content, sand content, exchangeable Ca, and exchangeable Mg.

In general, the highest SOM stocks (37.0 kg/ha) were found at the lowest soil depth (0–20 cm) and the lowest (7.7 kg/ha) at the deepest (40–60 cm), possibly due to the high decomposition rate of organic matter in the upper soil layers . The SOM stocks found in this study are considered low, even for the Brazilian Savannah, which is known as a semi-arid region with low organic matter content in the soil. Several studies that aimed to evaluate the C stocks in the no-tillage system in the Brazilian Savannah showed mean values of 44.5 mg/kg in the 0–5 cm layer and 35.9 mg/kg in the 5–10 cm layer .
The low SOM stocks found in the surface layers (0–20 and 20–40 cm) are concerning, since they indicate that the soil is subject to high degradation, due to the intense climate and use conditions. The reduction in SOM can generate a series of changes in the soil, such as a reduction in the number and diversity of soil organisms, changes in soil physical properties, such as a decrease in soil aggregate stability and an increase in soil penetration resistance and degradation of soil structure, which can reduce soil fertility and increase soil erosion and, consequently, reduce crop productivity and agricultural sustainability.
The low SOM values found in the soil of the Brazilian Savannah are associated with the characteristics of the climate, the type of native vegetation, land use and soil management. In general, the regions with semi-arid and tropical climates present low soil organic matter content, due to the high temperatures and the insolation, which promote organic matter decomposition . The reduction in soil organic matter content is more expressive in areas with native vegetation, since the native vegetation removal increases the incidence of solar radiation and the evapotranspiration, and promotes changes in the hydrological cycle, increasing the number of dry days and the length of the dry season

samples.hyp: The results also suggest that the role of forest cover as a key determinant of soil organic matter content in miombo woodlands is dependent on stand age. These findings have important implications for the management of miombo woodlands, particularly in the context of the on-going expansion of woodfuel and charcoal production in Africa (Machinga and Njoku 2007; Machinga et al. 2008). Due to the high demand for charcoal, small-scale producers have been increasing the extent and intensity of woodland burning, resulting in a decline in tree cover across the region (Sunderland and Kheng 2000; Machinga and Njoku 2007; Machinga et al. 2008; Campbell et al. 2013). Although there has been a growing body of research that has examined the effect of land use on soil organic matter in miombo woodlands (Sunderland and Kheng 2000; Machinga and Njoku 2007; Machinga et al. 2008; Campbell et al. 2013), few studies have considered how stand age and other stand-level variables contribute to soil organic matter content. Our results indicate that stand age and tree cover are important determinants of soil organic matter content in miombo woodlands, and that stand age alone explained 61% of the variation in soil organic matter content across the study sites. This finding has important implications for carbon sequestration and storage in miombo woodlands, particularly in the context of climate change mitigation through forest restoration and carbon farming (Sanchez 1999; Machinga and Njoku 2007; Machinga et al. 2008; Campbell et al. 2013). Our results suggest that miombo woodland management should consider stand age and tree cover as key determinants of soil organic matter content, and that soil organic matter content is likely to increase as woodland age increases. However, our results also suggest that, as woodland age increases, the effect of edaphic factors on soil organic matter content becomes less important. This finding should be considered when selecting sites for forest restoration and carbon farming projects in miombo woodlands, as it suggests that soil properties (edaphic factors) are less important for enhancing soil organic matter content in older stand ages. Our results also have implications for the management of small-scale charcoal production in miombo woodlands. Our results suggest that soil organic matter content is higher in secondary forests and woodlands compared to primary forests and woodlands

Scientists report that trees should be cut carefully in order to improve soil structure and fertility, and that the long-cherished belief that forests are the best carbon sinks is wrong.

Careful cutting of trees could help to improve soil structure and fertility, say scientists studying Zambian forests (pic: Rhett A. Butler)

Experts at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in Britain, working with colleagues at the University of Kuweit and the Zambia Agricultural Research Institute, studied three different plots of land in Zambia’s Sinthunzi Forest Reserve.

One was left untouched as a control, one was subject to selective cutting of trees – keeping a mix of ages and types, and the third was subject to the cutting of all trees over 10cm in diameter.

After 18 months, the scientists took soil samples and found that although all three plots showed improvements in some areas of soil health, the third showed greatest gains.

The scientists, whose work is published in the journal Global Change Biology, say that the long-held belief that forests are the best carbon sinks is wrong.

They say the reason for this is that it is not just about the carbon: it is the combination of tree species and the structure from years of tree growth that determine the health of the soil.

Dr. Jefferson L. Kubuya of the University of East Anglia said: “Sustainable forest management is really important in order to maintain forest ecosystem services like water and air quality, and regulation of the climate.

“People often think that leaving the forest intact is the best way to protect it, but our results suggest that carefully selective cutting to create a mosaic of age classes can actually promote a healthier forest and soil, improving its ability to regulate water.”

Professor Pierre L. A. Maillard of the University of East Anglia added: “Our results suggest that it is not only the trees that should be left when managing our forests, but also the dead wood, which is important for fungi breakdown and for providing habitat for many species of animals, and the shrubs, which are important for many pollinators such as bees and birds.”

They found that the soils in this region contained an average of 29,000 kilograms (kg) of carbon per hectare, which is more than double the amount found in surrounding forests and is also higher than the global average for temperate and tropical regions.

These findings suggest that the original forest in this region was probably much more extensive than previous studies estimated.

The researchers also found that the soils in secondary forests and agricultural land in the region contain less carbon than primary forest soils, which suggests that deforestation and agricultural expansion in the Copperbelt is reducing the region’s ability to sequester carbon.

Deforestation is also reducing the ability of the remaining primary forests in the region to store carbon, the researchers say.

The researchers used satellite imagery to determine how much tree cover had changed since 1984 in the study area, which is located to the west of the Copperbelt, the mineral-rich region that stretches across Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

They found that the area contained 2.2 million hectares of tree cover in 1984, and by 2018 this had been reduced by 30% to 1.5 million hectares. The loss of tree cover in this region is primarily the result of logging and agricultural expansion.

The researchers also measured the amount of carbon stored in the top 30 centimeters of soil from 268 collection sites in the Copperbelt, and from 60 sites in nearby primary and secondary forests.

They found that the soils in the forest had an average of 29,000 kg of carbon per hectare, while the secondary forest and agricultural land contained an average of 22,000 kg and 19,000 kg of carbon per hectare, respectively. (All together, the researchers collected soil samples from over 1,400 sites across the Copperbelt.)

The difference between the primary forest and secondary forest/soil agricultural land is likely due to differences in the amount of organic matter preserved in the soil, the researchers say.

The amount of organic matter in a soil is usually measured by the amount of carbon it contains. This is measured in parts per million (ppm) or percent of the soil weight. Most prairie soils contain 3 to 6% organic matter and some claypan soils contain as much as 10%. Compost can add from 0.5% to over 5% organic matter to a soil. Adding 1% organic matter to a soil increases the capacity of the soil to retain water and nutrients by about 1%. Adding 1 pound of compost per square foot will usually result in a 1% increase in organic matter in the soil.

The organic matter in the soil is important for many reasons. Organic matter affects the physical properties of the soil. Soils high in organic matter are usually more open and less compact. The pores between the soil particles hold water and air. Soils high in organic matter usually have better aeration and greater water-holding capacity. The organic matter in the soil also affects the chemical properties of the soil. Organic matter contains nutrients needed for plant growth. A large part of the nutrients added to a soil as fertilizer are held in the organic matter. The organic matter also helps make other nutrients available to plants. Organic matter also helps make the nutrients in the soil less likely to be lost through runoff or leaching. The organic matter in the soil also affects the biological properties of the soil. The billions of soil microorganisms in a pound of soil need the carbon from the organic matter to build their cells. Microbes break down the organic matter, and in the process they add nutrients to the soil. Microbes also help make nutrients available to plants. They do this by secreting enzymes that convert organic nutrients into a form that plants can take up through their roots. The microbes also form associations with some plant roots that allow them to receive nutrients from the microbes and protect the microbes from being killed by the plant’s toxins.

The microorganisms in a pound of soil may come from as many as 25,000 different species. Earthworms, grubs, and other soil invertebrates mix the organic matter into the soil and as they move through the soil they add oxygen to it.

Soils of Brazil Observatory

The program is divided into two projects: the Soils of Brazil (Vegetal Cover and Use) Survey, a traditional soil survey using field work and soil description in the field; and the Soils of Brazil Database, which brings together information from various sources, such as the mapping of soil classes and the distribution of land use.

“We used the database to select the locations of the study sites. We took soil samples at depths of 5 cm, 10 cm and 20 cm at each of the 50 study sites, which were distributed across six Brazilian biomes [ejunto, pampa, pantanal, cerrado, Atlantic Forest and Amazon Forest],” Silva Filho said.

Chickpea is an important crop for food security and income in Ethiopia. However, the average yield is only 4–6 tha−1 compared to the theoretical yield potential of 50 tha−1. The national average of insecticide use for the control of different insect pests in chickpea is 2.67 kg ha−1, fungicide use is 0.76 kg ha−1, and use of different types of herbicides is 2.05 kg ha−1 (Deogratias et al., 2020). The high use of pesticides is due to the high prevalence of pests, diseases, and abiotic stresses, which are responsible for 50% grain yield loss (Boukar et al., 1999; Kumar et al., 2017). The biotic stresses include insects such as callosobrochas anrenigera, Helicoverpa armigera, Sitophilus oryzae, and Trogoderma granarium, among others, and diseases such as Ascochyta rabiei, Leptosphaeria maculans, and Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Amanullah et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2017). To achieve the green revolution in Ethiopia, there is an urgent need to develop improved varieties with tolerance to abiotic stress, resistance to biotic stresses, and high yield potential. One of the best ways to develop improved varieties is to combine the efforts of different stakeholders through the innovation platform approach.

The innovation platform is a new approach that brings together different public and private sector stakeholders who can contribute to crop improvement through their core competencies (Crouch and Smith, 2001). The concept was initiated by the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR) in 2000 and later by the Global Crop Diversity Trust (2015) and the Alliance of Digital Agriculture (2016). The innovation platform approach has been successfully used in maize (Fregene et al., 2016), banana (Kfir et al., 2018), and wheat (Liu et al., 2020). The innovation platform is a powerful tool to promote multi-actor innovation and collaborative decision-making in agriculture (Hartley et al., 2020). The innovation platform approach has not yet been used for crop improvement of chickpea, which is an important and staple food crop in Ethiopia.

The Platform was established in the framework of the International Collaborative Research Projects (ICRP) funded by the CGIAR Fund.

The Platform is open to all stakeholders involved in the chickpea value chain, in particular:

  • breeders,
  • pathologists,
  • agronomists,
  • seed companies,
  • processors,
  • traders,
  • farmers.

The Platform activities include:

  • exchange of information on challenges and opportunities in the chickpea research and development,
  • standardization of methods of evaluation of breeding materials and germplasm,
  • organized participation of the private sector in the international multi-location trials,
  • capacity building,
  • and identification of the priorities for research and development.

samples.src: How Ethiopia boosted chickpea production
samples.ref: I-Ethiopia ikhulise kanjani ukukhiqizwa kwe-chickpea
samples.hyp:
and exports

Chickpeas are an important crop for Ethiopia, providing food security, income, and foreign exchange. However, production is subject to major yield constraints, with wide variations in yield across farms. To address this, researchers tested different rates of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) application, as well as different planting configurations, to identify production enhancements that could increase yields and support the expansion of chickpea cultivation. 

In a long-term site, experiments tested different N and P rates in combination with the previous crop residue (maize) and no previous crop residue. The number of rows per plant was also tested, with one farm using 10 rows per plant and another using 20. The results showed that:

  • Retaining previous crop residue increased yields by 40%, from 498 to 695kg/ha, and this was the highest yield in the experiment.
  • The optimal combination of N and P was 100kg/ha of N and 50kg/ha of P.
  • The number of rows per plant did not have a significant effect on yield.

These findings suggest that:

  • Maintaining crop residue is an easy and effective way to increase chickpea yields.
  • The number of rows per plant does not need to be managed, as having more rows did not lead to a significant increase in yield.
  • For optimal nutrient input, farmers should use 100kg/ha of N and 50kg/ha of P.

To support these recommendations, further research is needed to investigate the macro and micro nutrients that could enhance chickpea production, as well as to conduct on-farm trials to validate the findings from the long-term experiment.

Agricultural research organisation, the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), says it has successfully trained 1,500 farmers in Malawi on the production of drought-tolerant chickpeas.

The institute said the training was done virtually and physically through its Kala Huweka platform, which was launched in June 2021.

The authors said the platform made sure that farmers were trained to increase their knowledge on chickpea production.

The training was conducted in three districts in Malawi, namely Lilongwe, Salima, and Dedza.

The institute said the training was aimed at increasing the knowledge of farmers on good agronomic practices, post-harvest management, and market access.

The authors said that the training was also aimed at increasing the income of farmers through the production of quality seeds and value addition.

The institute said it partnered with the National Food Reserve Agency (NFRA) and Malawi Grain Traders Association (MaGTA) to ensure that the produced seeds are linked to markets and also stocked in NFRA silos for government to purchase during times of food crisis.

The University of Washington’s Global Health Institute has launched a new initiative to track the genetic changes of the coronavirus as it spreads around the world.

The project, led by the UW Bioengineering and the Institute for Protein Design, aims to sequence and analyze 1000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected from around the world each week to understand how the virus is evolving and to help inform public health decisions.

Scientists track how coronavirus variants change so that they can better understand how well vaccines might work against new variants. (Pexels / Unsplash), CC0, via Pexels

The effort is part of a larger global collaboration called Next Strain that shares data on coronavirus genomic sequences with public health officials and researchers around the world.

The UW team will focus on three areas.

The first is tracking the genetic changes of the coronavirus in countries hit the hardest by the pandemic, such as the United States, India, and Brazil, where new variants have contributed to a rapid rise in COVID-19 cases this year.

The second is sequencing viruses from around the world to understand how the virus is evolving and to inform vaccine design and the development of treatments.

The third is building a global network of researchers in public health, infectious diseases, and health equity to ensure the project is representing the global impact of the coronavirus.

“Understanding how SARS-CoV-2 is evolving is critical to keep the pandemic from escalating again,” said Bryan Brina, a UW research assistant professor of bioengineering and of molecular & cellular pharmacology, in a statement. “This project brings together the unique strengths of the UW and the Seattle Bioengineering department to sequence samples quickly and contribute new scientific insights that will aid the global response to the pandemic.”

The project also aims to understand how factors such as population dynamics, health care systems, social infrastructure, and climate affect the spread of the coronavirus.

The UW team is partnering with the COVID-19 Genomics Consortium U.S. and BEI Genomics, a company that provides SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequencing services to more than 40 state and local health departments.

The authors sequence 110 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from 46 patients in Sudan, identifying 13 unique genomes. They also analyze the titer and neutralization capacity of 194 plasma samples collected from convalescent patients between April and October 2020. While the authors report a number of interesting findings, the data has some limitations. First, the authors do not describe the case-fatality rate of the patients included in this study. This is a key piece of information to help put the findings in context for the reader. Second, the authors report that 3 of 194 plasma samples were positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR, but that viral loads were low and these samples showed high neutralization activity. It is not clear why these samples were included in the study, as they may not be representative of samples collected during natural infection. Third, the authors do not include a date of specimen collection for the plasma samples included in this study. It is unclear why this information is missing, but it makes it difficult for the reader to interpret the neutralization data in the context of when the samples were collected and the evolving SARS-CoV-2 variants in the country. Fourth, the lack of demographic information about the patients included in this study limits the discussion of the findings. Finally, the authors do not include a methods section in their manuscript. A detailed description of the sequencing and neutralization assay methods would allow other researchers to reproduce these findings with ease.

The authors identify 13 unique SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Sudan. The authors use a phylogenetic tree to show that 11/13 of the unique genomes are more closely related to variants first identified in Europe than to variants first identified in Africa or Asia. This finding is interesting as it suggests that importation of SARS-CoV-2 from another continent rather than local transmission occurred more often. However, the authors do not include a date of specimen collection for their patients, making it difficult to assess the timing of import versus local transmission. In addition, the authors include 3 plasma samples from patients who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR. These samples may have been collected after other patients, which would have given locals more time to transmit the virus. samples.hyp:
The Evolution of Sex Differences in Health and Disease

What Makes a Woman? The Evolution of Sex Differences in Health and Disease

by Nancy Segal and Andrew Z. Hillman

The sex of a person – his or her biological sex – is determined by the combination of chromosomes that he or she inherits from his or her parents. Females have two X chromosomes, while males have an X and a Y chromosome. The presence of the Y chromosome determines that an individual will be male, and the absence of the Y chromosome determines that an individual will be female. The primary physical differences between males and females are thus explained by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome. The presence of the Y chromosome during embryonic development causes the undifferentiated gonads to develop into testes, which produce androgens, such as testosterone. These androgens, in turn, produce the secondary physical differences between males and females, such as broader shoulders, larger lungs, and more muscle mass in males, and wider hips, more body fat, and less muscle mass in females. These differences are illustrated in Figure 1.1. However, sex is not simply the sum of an individual’s sex chromosomes or sex hormones. Rather, sex is a complex and interactive web of hormones, chromosomes, neural sex differences, and social environment that change across the lifespan.

Figure 1.1. Primary and secondary sex differences between men and women. Primary sex differences are due to the presence of the Y chromosome, which directs the developing fetus to develop into a male. Secondary sex differences are due to testosterone and other androgens produced by the testes that the fetus develops into a male. (Segal and Hillman, 2020)

Evolutionary theories of sex differences have changed numerous times since their inception, and these changes have often reflected the prevailing scientific paradigms of their time. Early evolutionary theories of the late 19th and early 20th centuries focused on natural selection as the primary mechanism producing sex differences. Under this framework, the application of Darwinian natural selection pressure to issues of gender produced a theory of sexual selection, in which reproductive success (i.e., producing as many viable offspring as possible) became a key concept. This early theory of sexual selection was sex-biased, focusing on the reproductive success of males, and specifically on the number of mates and offspring that a male could have. This approach was criticized for its reduction of females to “passive receptacles” and for ignoring the fact that females invest more resources in their offspring

Case studies were conducted as part of a larger research project entitled “Documenting the Reasons for and Circumstances of Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting in Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya.” This report aims to present the results of the case studies conducted in each country and to document the reasons and circumstances surrounding the continuation of FGM/C in each setting. The research was conducted in 2016 by the Center for Health and Socio-Economic Development (CHSED) in collaboration with the African Studies Center, both at Addis Ababa University in Ethiopia; the Interfaith Dialogue for Peace (IDP) in Indonesia; and the African Population and Health Research Center (APHRC) in Kenya. The research was funded by the United Nations Trust Fund to End Violence against Women.

In selecting countries, we aimed to include settings with varying prevalence and severity of FGM/C as well as different religious and cultural contexts. The research team, in collaboration with each partner, identified in-country partners, defined study sites, and conducted fieldwork. In all countries, the research team members and in-country partners worked closely together, ensuring that ethical guidelines and consent were upheld. In Indonesia, the research was conducted in two settings in two provinces: East Java and North Sumatra. In each location, four focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted with women who had undergone FGM/C and girls who had not yet undergone FGM/C. In addition, individual in-depth interviews were conducted with key informants, including religious leaders, members of anti-FGM/C organizations, and members of FGM/C practitioner associations. In Ethiopia, the research was conducted in three rural districts in two regions: Afar and Somali. In each district, four FGDs were held with women who had undergone FGM/C and girls who had not yet undergone FGM/C. In addition, individual in-depth interviews were conducted with key informants, including mothers, fathers, and anti-FGM/C activists. samples.hyp:
The analysis presented here draws on the household survey and focus group discussions with young people. The survey was a two-stage cluster sample survey with a sample of 9,282 young people aged 15-24 years. In the first stage, 2,400 clusters were selected with probability proportional to population size. In the second stage, 30 households per cluster were selected with equal probability. The survey questionnaire covered a range of topics including socio-demographics, exposure to media and information, knowledge of contraception, attitudes towards contraception, and contraceptive use. The focus group discussions were held with young people (aged 15-24 years) and community members (aged 18 years and over) in each district. There were 67 focus group discussions with young people (3 in each community: 2 with males, 1 with females) and 33 focus group discussions with community members (1 in each community). In all, 20 in-depth interviews were also conducted with young people and community stakeholders, and 14 key informant interviews with community stakeholders were conducted. The in-depth interviews and key informant interviews were conducted with purposefully selected stakeholders in each district. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Botswana and the Botswana Government Ethics Committee. All interviewees signed informed consent forms prior to participation in the study. Participants’ confidentiality was protected by using pseudonyms in the analysis and by limiting access to the data. All data collected are kept at the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program database at ICF Meta and the Botswana DHS website.

samples.src: Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were conducted.
samples.ref: Izibalo ezichazayo nokuhlaziywa kokuqukethwe kwendikimba zenziwa.
samples.hyp:
Descriptive statistics included means and frequencies of demographic and other variables. Thematic content analysis of open-ended questions was conducted by coding response content to specific domains of interest and subdomains within those domains. Specifically, for the open-ended knowledge and awareness questions, we coded for correct, partially correct, and no/incorrect responses. For example, response content for the question “What is the definition of a pandemic?” was coded to the subdomains of “incorrect”, “contagious spread of a disease”, “involves international spread of a disease”, and “more than one country involved”. For the open-ended perception of risk questions, we coded for “perceived risk”, “no risk”, and “not a risk to me”. For example, response content for the question “How big of a risk do you think the coronavirus health crisis is to you and your family?” was coded to the subdomains of “no risk”, “slightly high risk”, “high risk”, and “don’t know”. For the open-ended questions about sources of information, we coded for specific media channels, social media platforms, and personal contacts. We also conducted exploratory factor analysis to identify a smaller number of underlying risk perception factors that explained the variation in response content. Finally, bivariate and multivariate statistical analyses were conducted to identify associations between demographic variables and specific domains or subdomains of response content. For the bivariate analyses, we conducted Pearson’s correlations for the continuous variables and Chi-square for the categorical variables. For the multivariate analyses, we conducted multiple linear regression analyses with the continuous variables and multiple logistic regression analyses with the categorical variables. We used the SPSS version 24 and R statistical software to conduct our analyses. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of the University of the Western Cape (protocol number: 2019-00509-2500).

To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it’s happening

Research into the reasons behind female genital mutilation is growing. This could be the key to ending the practice

Eve Sillera/Getty Images

Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a global problem, with thousands of girls cut every year, mostly in Africa. In Somalia and Egypt, 98% and 97% of girls are cut, respectively. Even in the UK, where the practice is illegal, up to 60,000 girls are subjected to FGM every year.

But after years of campaigning by charities and governments, the number of girls being cut each year is falling. In Egypt, 87% of girls aged 14 to 49 have undergone FGM, down from 91% in 2008. In Somalia, 56% of girls aged 15 to 49 have been cut, down from 98% in 2000.

So, is FGM on the decline? Not necessarily. “There are different trends in different countries,” says Adeeb Hajo, a medical anthropologist at the University of Illinois in Chicago.

In some countries, like Egypt, the rate of decline is slowing. In others, like Djibouti, the rate of decline is increasing. But overall, the trend is positive, says Hajo. “The question is, can we make it faster?”

To make FGM disappear, we first need to understand why it exists. Many people assume that FGM is a straightforward matter of tradition, or that it is linked to cultural or religious beliefs. But the reality is more complex.

There is no single reason why FGM exists. It occurs in diverse communities with different values and beliefs. “It’s a range of factors that come together in different ways in different contexts,” says Siwan Muthaly, a medical anthropologist at the University of Sussex in the UK.

Other reasons for FGM are more practical. For example, some communities believe that FGM will make girls more attractive to potential husbands, or that it will increase their chances of getting married. In some cases, FGM is performed because it is expected by the girl’s family or community.

samples.src: Reproductive Hormones Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultrastructural Changes in Testis of African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
samples.ref: Ukungalingani Kwama-Hormone Enzalo, I-Germ Cell Apoptosis, I-Sperm Morphophenotypes Engavamile kanye Nezinguquko Ezinhle Kakhulu Kumagundane Amakhulu Ase-Afrika (Cricetomys gaambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Echayeke Ku-Sodium Metavanadate Ukudakwa
samples.hyp:
The effects of sodium metavanadate (NaMO) on the male reproductive system of African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus) were investigated. Animals were divided into four groups and treated as follows: group I served as control; group II was administered NaMO at a single dose of 10 mg/kg body weight; group III received NaMO at a single dose of 20 mg/kg body weight; and group IV was administered NaMO at a double dose (10 mg/kg body weight for two consecutive days). After 15 days of exposure, all animals were euthanized, and their reproductive organs were removed, dissected, and processed for light and scanning electron microscopy. Our results showed that NaMO exposure induced a significant decrease in body weight and testis weight in all treated groups compared to the control. The testis to body weight ratio was significantly decreased in groups III and IV. Testis sections from control animals showed normal seminiferous tubule sections with the presence of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids, and round spermatids. In NaMO-treated animals, a number of structural changes were observed in seminiferous tubules, such as vacuolization, detachment of spermatogonia from the basal membrane, and the presence of apoptotic bodies, all of which are signs of germ cell apoptosis. In addition, abnormal sperm morphophenotypes were observed in the lumen of seminiferous tubules, such as round, smooth-head, and multi-nucleated spermatids, and detached elongated spermatids. These findings indicate that NaMO exposure induces reproductive hormones imbalance, germ cell apoptosis, and abnormal sperm morphophenotypes in the testis of African giant rats, which may lead to male infertility.

This is due to the increase in the vanadium mining and processing in South Africa. The aim of this study was to establish the levels of vanadium in various parts of the body of vanadium mine workers, and to determine the factors that may influence the absorption and excretion of vanadium in the body. A total of 102 male mine workers, aged 25 to 65, were randomly selected from the workforce of three different vanadium mines in South Africa. The participants provided a blood and urine sample, which was analyzed for the concentration of vanadium. The average concentration of vanadium in blood and urine were 3.46 ± 2.12 μg/L and 5.77 ± 6.6 μg/L, respectively. The concentration of vanadium in the different groups was statistically similar. There was no correlation between the concentration of vanadium in blood and the concentration of vanadium in urine. The results of this study show that the concentration of vanadium in mine workers is much higher than the average concentration found in the general population. Mine workers are likely to be exposed to higher levels of vanadium than other occupational groups. Therefore, further research should concentrate on the long-term effects of exposure to low levels of vanadium.

At the end of the treatment period, animals were sacrificed and the small intestine was removed, rinsed with ice-cold saline, pat dried and the length of the sample was measured. The sample was divided into 3 equal parts. The middle part of the sample was used for microanatomy and the two other parts were used for the isolation of villi. The two parts were immersed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1M cacodylate buffer at 4°C. After 48 h, the tissues were washed 3 times in the same buffer and then immersed in 1% osmium tetroxide solution in the same buffer at 4°C for 72 h. The samples were then washed 3 times in the same buffer and dehydrated in an ascending series of ethanol. The samples were then immersed in propylene oxide and the propylene oxide-embedded tissue was transferred to a pure acetone bottle. The samples were then embedded in epoxy resin, hardened for 48 h at 70°C and sectioned into 2 μm thick sections. The sections were collected on glass slides and stained with 1% toluidine blue solution. The stained sections were examined using a light microscope and photographs were taken. The microvilli were measured using a light microscope connected to a digital camera. The height and surface area of the microvilli were measured and the data were analyzed using the SPSS version 11.5. Differences between the means of the groups were assessed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and significant differences were further assessed by Tukey’s test. P < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.

The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the University of the Free State (UFS), South Africa (Application number: 1754).
