The study appears in ACS' journal Environmental Science & Technology.

Xu and colleagues note that nanosilver is used in a wide range of consumer products, including textiles and footwear, medical devices and wound dressings. It also is used as a coating on building materials, such as tiles, to protect them from microbial growth and in water treatment systems to prevent the growth of bacteria, mold and algae. Concerns about the environmental fate and transport of nanosilver have grown as the use of products containing nanosilver increases. Previous studies have shown that nanosilver is toxic to a variety of organisms including bacteria, algae, invertebrates and vertebrates. However, the researchers say very little is known about the toxicological effects of nanosilver on human health.

To better understand the risks, the scientists first reviewed other studies on the topic. Then, they exposed groups of human lung cells to different concentrations of nanosilver to discover which genes might be activated and regulate the toxic effects of the material. The researchers also investigated whether the composition of the cells, which can vary between men and women, and among people of different ages, affected the nanosilver's toxicity. Finally, they compared the lung cells' response to nanosilver with their response to titanium dioxide, a similar material that also has been found in the environment.

They found that common gene-signature responses to nanosilver exposure were very similar to those for titanium dioxide, which suggests certain key signaling pathways may be important in the toxicity of both materials. The researchers also identified 69 genes that were affected by nanosilver and two main groups of genes that appeared to regulate the material's toxicity. Additionally, the scientists determined that the toxicity of nanosilver did not differ significantly between male and female cells. While more work is needed, the study provides important new information that can be used to develop tests for evaluating the potential health effects of nanosilver and other materials.

samples.hyp:
The present study was designed to investigate the effects of vanadium on reproduction of Wistar rats. METHODS: The study was carried out on 40 male and female rats, divided into four groups viz. control group (group I), and three treated groups (II, III and IV) each comprising 10 rats. The test compound vanadium was administered at 100, 200 and 400 micro g/kg body weight to the treated groups III and IV orally for 30 consecutive days. At the end of the experiment, all the rats were dissected and their ovaries were removed, cleared, desiccated and weighed. RESULTS: The results of the present study showed significant decrease (p<0.05) in body weight of the rats in the treated groups in comparison to the control group. There was a significant decrease (p<0.05) in the weight of the ovaries in the treated groups in comparison to the control group. CONCLUSION: The results of the present study indicate that vanadium at the dose of 100 micro g/kg body weight causes some adverse effects on the reproductive system of the rats.

The research was recently published in the open access journal Environmental Science Europe.

The authors of this study have used a new approach to analyse samples from fish caught in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of Brazil. They found that fish from more polluted waters had shorter telomeres, which are sections of protective protein at the end of our chromosomes. Shortened telomeres have been shown in previous studies to be an indicator of stress, and in this case the scientists suspect that pollution is the stressor.

Telomeres are protective caps on the ends of our chromosomes, a bit like the plastic tips at the end of your hair that stop it from breaking. They consist of a series of simple DNA sequences that are repeated thousands of times, and the protein trithorax, which helps to keep them intact. Telomeres get shorter every time our cells divide, and once they get too short, the chromosomes are put at risk of damage. This can lead to errors in cell division that may lead to cancer.

Larger fish from less polluted waters had longer telomeres in their blood cells than smaller fish from more polluted waters.

The difference in telomere length between large and small fish caught in more polluted waters was about 1,600 DNA repeats – quite a significant difference when you consider that the telomeres of the largest fish caught were only 7,500 repeats long.

The researchers also looked for the protein trithorax near the telomeres, and found that in fish from less polluted waters it was present at high levels, almost always covering the end of the chromosome. By contrast, in fish from more polluted waters, trithorax coverage was much lower, and was more often missing from the very end of the chromosome, where telomeres are located.

Dr. Elvira de Oliveira from the Federal University of Parana, Brazil, is the corresponding author of the study. She said “Telomere reduction is a marker of environmental stress caused by pollution in fish, and this can be used to indicate the effects of environmental contamination to wildlife and possibly to humans as well.”

Dr. Salvador Viaene from the University of Evora, Portugal, co-authored the study. He said “Telomeres are sensitive indicators of the effects of pollution. Our results suggest that short telomeres are a sign of high pollution levels, and that telomere length measurement could be used as a biomarker for environmental monitoring programs.”

samples.hyp:
The aim of this study was to assess the floristic composition of homegardens in the district. Data were collected from 48 homegardens in the district. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), Kruskal–Wallis tests, and multivariate analyses of variance (MANOVA). A total of 89 woody and herbaceous plant species from 25 families were recorded in the homegardens. The woody species were dominated by trees (47.19%) followed by shrubs (32.91%) and lianas (19.90%). The families Poaceae, Rosaceae, and Rubiaceae contributed the most to the floristic composition of the homegardens. The results of the MANOVA and NMDS indicated that the homegarden owners in the district used 17.75% native and 82.25% introduced plant species. The homegardens in the district were found to be a mixture of both, indigenous and introduced species. Therefore, homegardens in the district can be considered as a potential reservoir of both indigenous and introduced plant species.

Homegardens are a significant source of food and other products to millions of people in the tropics (Garcia et al., 2011). Homegardens are recognized as one of the most important _diversity_ in the world (Rundel & Rundel, 2002). In addition to being a source of food, homegardens provide a range of non-timber forest products such as dyes, medicines, and crafts (Tchouta et al., 2014). Homegardens are also significant for their spiritual and religious value (Tchouta et al., 2014). Homegardens are associated with a number of cultural practices and have been described as a _living_ (Morton, 1987). The plants in homegardens have been found to have a number of uses and are also considered to have aesthetic value (Tchouta et al., 2014). Homegardens are often established in areas with poor soils and little water, and are able to grow a variety of plants that provide food and other products (Garcia et al., 2011). The plants in homegardens are also found to have a number of other benefits, such as providing shade and protecting against soil erosion (Tchouta et al., 2014). Homegardens are an important part of the cultural landscape in many parts of the world and are worth preserving for their cultural, ecological, and economic value.

In this study, we aimed to identify the main factors that influence the management of homegardens by the Bribri, an indigenous group from Talamanca, Costa Rica. We conducted 47 semi-structured interviews to characterize the homegardens and to identify the main factors that influence the management of homegardens. We analyzed the data using inductive approaches. Results showed that Bribri's homegardens are small in size (0.17±0.54ha), highly diversified (14.28±5.78 species/ha) and mostly located in the upper parts of the mountains (950-1100mmsl). The most diverse crops were cacao (Theobroma cacao), coconut (Cocos nucifera), breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis), and pepper (Piper grossum). The main factors that influence the management of homegardens were: (i) cultural factors, which are the most important, such as the need to collect food, medicine, and other products from the homegardens, the cultural belief that the forest and the homegarden are a single entity, and the cultural practice of maintaining a forest garden; (ii) biological factors, such as the homegarden's edge effect and the beneficial properties of some species; (iii) economic factors, such as the homegarden's contribution to family income and the sale of agricultural products from the homegarden; and (iv) structural factors, such as the presence of a spring on the property. Structural equations models identified that the cultural factors are the main determinants of biodiversity in homegardens. This study improves our understanding about the main factors that influence the management of homegardens by the Bribri, an indigenous group from Talamanca, Costa Rica.

Ethiopian gardens support food security and conservation

A UBC botanist and her team of local collaborators have found that home gardens in Ethiopia play an important role in providing food and conservation value to the country’s capital city.

The study, led by UBC botanist Bruce McCann, is the first to characterize the plant species found in household gardens in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. The research team consisted of botanists from UBC and the University of Bahir Dar, as well as horticultural experts from Addis Acqua Greening PLC, a company that designs and installs green infrastructure in the city.

The study was published this month in the journal Applied Geography.

“Gardens are often overlooked as they don’t fit into the agricultural or wildland categories, but they can play an important role in food security and conservation,” says McCann, a professor in the UBC Department of Botany.

The researchers visited 122 gardens in Addis Ababa and identified 137 different plant species that were grown for food, ornamental purposes, or both. The study found that gardeners grew 71 native and 66 non-native plant species. The most commonly grown species were non-native, including local varieties of fruit trees such as avocado, orange, lemon and mango.

“Non-native species are often seen as a drain on biodiversity, but in this case they are providing an important source of food and income for the people of Addis Ababa,” says McCann.

The study also found that native species, such as coffee and honeybee plants, were grown to contribute to Ethiopia’s conservation and tourism efforts. Ethiopia is home to a high number of endemic plant and animal species, and the country has made conservation a high priority.

“Addis Ababa is growing rapidly, so it’s important that its green spaces contribute to both food and conservation security,” says McCann. “Our results can help inform green infrastructure projects in the city by identifying which plant species should be preserved and which should be removed to allow for new developments.”

“Farmers are growing food and other plants that they can sell and make an income from,” she said. 

The study also found that farmers grow different varieties of the same plant for various purposes. 

“Farmers grow different varieties of maize for different purposes,” she said. “Some they use for consumption, some they use for sale and others they use for traditional purposes like making beer.” 

The researchers said they found that farmers prefer to grow plants that have multiple uses, such as maize and bananas. 

“Just a few examples of multiple use plants are banana, maize, manioc and beans,” she said. 

The study also found that farmers obtain plant seeds from a variety of places. 

“Farmers obtain seeds from places such as their own fields, from relatives, from neighbors, from the local market, from fellow farmers and from agricultural extension workers,” she said. 

Further, the study found that farmers store their seeds in different ways. 

“Farmers store seeds in places such as their own houses, in the fields, in the kitchen, in godowns and with their neighbors,” she said.

This difference could be because the other study looked at all plants, not just herbs. It is also possible that the other study looked at plants that had been growing for a long time, and that the plants grown by farmers for medicine are shorter-lived. To check on this, the researchers did a separate study looking at all the plants in the area. They found that the other study was correct—trees and shrubs were more common in the area than herbs. This shows that the original study had limitations, even though the questions and methods were good.
